  Novel Approach
abstract:
CPU performance prediction, which involves forecasting the performance scores
of a CPU based on its hardware characteristics during its operation, is a
critical technology for computational system design and resource management in
the big data era. However, this research field currently faces two significant
challenges. First, collecting real-world data is challenging due to the wide
variety of CPU products on the market and the highly specialized nature of
relevant hardware characteristics. In the research process, this field lacks a
standard dataset with unified hardware characteristics, wide data coverage, and
comprehensive benchmarks. Second, existing methods based on hardware simulation
models or machine learning exhibit notable shortcomings, such as lengthy
simulation test cycles and low prediction accuracy. To bridge these gaps, we
first collect, preprocess, and standardize historical data from the 4th
Generation Intel Xeon Scalable Processors across multiple benchmark suites to
create a new dataset, named PerfCastDB. Subsequently, we design a deep learning
based model called Nova CPU Performance Predictor (NCPP) as the baseline for
this new dataset. The NCPP network is designed based on group attention
mechanism. It effectively quantifies the implicit relationships between
hardware characteristics within and across groups and comprehensively models
the impact of various hardware characteristics on CPU performance prediction.
We conduct comparative experiments using the proposed PerfCastDB dataset.
Compared to existing approaches, NCPP achieves superior evaluation results,
demonstrating its effectiveness. Furthermore, we have open-sourced part of the
dataset and the NCPP network code to facilitate subsequent research. The
resources can be accessed at https://github.com/xiaoman-liu/NCPP.
estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

title: Pipeline-Native Transformers: Co-Designing Model Architecture and CPU Inference for Bandwidth-Efficient Autoregressive Decode
abstract:
Single-token autoregressive decode on CPUs is bound by memory bandwidth, not arithmetic: a modern CPU sustains roughly 1 TFLOP/s of compute but only about 50 GB/s from main memory, and each generated token must stream every active weight once. This report argues that the most effective response is to co-design the model architecture and the inference runtime together. It presents cflow, a CPU-first streaming engine, alongside a family of pipeline-native transformer architectures whose inter-layer dependency graphs are constructed to permit a vertical, stage-major execution schedule.
  cflow stores weights as L2-sized tiles in compute-consumption order, reads only the top-k experts of each mixture-of-experts layer, fuses projections, and executes a delay-aware schedule from per-model dependency parameters. Across five architectures trained on TinyStories, one (arch2_4_combined) achieves a 2.00x reduction in critical-path weight bandwidth (9.00 to 4.50 MB/token) within 0.24 perplexity of the best candidate, and the tile layout incurs 7.29x fewer L1-data read misses than a row-major baseline. On a 30.9-billion-parameter pipeline-native MoE, cflow decodes at 5.94 tokens/s (tok/s) on a 32-vCPU Ice Lake server, ahead of llama.cpp (4.75) and the vLLM CPU backend (1.65) on comparably sized dense models. Realizing the expert-delay window as asynchronous I/O overlap on a disk-resident expert tier yields a further net win of up to 1.68x, matching the overlap model within 1%. Measurement refutes one of the eight design claims and leaves a second inconclusive; both are reported in full, with the conditions under which they would hold.
estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

title:
HybriMoE: Hybrid CPU-GPU Scheduling and Cache Management for Efficient
  MoE Inference
abstract:
The Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture has demonstrated significant
advantages as it enables to increase the model capacity without a proportional
increase in computation. However, the large MoE model size still introduces
substantial memory demands, which usually requires expert offloading on
resource-constrained platforms and incurs significant overhead. Hybrid CPU-GPU
inference has been proposed to leverage CPU computation to reduce expert
loading overhead but faces major challenges: on one hand, the expert activation
patterns of MoE models are highly unstable, rendering the fixed mapping
strategies in existing works inefficient; on the other hand, the hybrid CPU-GPU
schedule for MoE is inherently complex due to the diverse expert sizes,
structures, uneven workload distribution, etc. To address these challenges, in
this paper, we propose HybriMoE, a hybrid CPU-GPU inference framework that
improves resource utilization through a novel CPU-GPU scheduling and cache
management system. HybriMoE introduces (i) a dynamic intra-layer scheduling
strategy to balance workloads across CPU and GPU, (ii) an impact-driven
inter-layer prefetching algorithm, and (iii) a score-based caching algorithm to
mitigate expert activation instability. We implement HybriMoE on top of the
kTransformers framework and evaluate it on three widely used MoE-based LLMs.
Experimental results demonstrate that HybriMoE achieves an average speedup of
1.33times in the prefill stage and 1.70times in the decode stage compared
to state-of-the-art hybrid MoE inference framework. Our code is available at:
https://github.com/PKU-SEC-Lab/HybriMoE.
estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

title: Extending Puzzle for Mixture-of-Experts Reasoning Models with Application to GPT-OSS Acceleration
abstract: Reasoning-focused LLMs improve answer quality by generating longer reasoning traces, but the additional tokens dramatically increase serving cost, motivating inference optimization. We extend and apply Puzzle, a post-training neural architecture search (NAS) framework, to gpt-oss-120B to produce gpt-oss-puzzle-88B, a deployment-optimized derivative. Our approach combines heterogeneous MoE expert pruning, selective replacement of full-context attention with window attention, FP8 KV-cache quantization with calibrated scales, and post-training reinforcement learning to recover accuracy, while maintaining low generation length. In terms of per-token speeds, on an 8XH100 node we achieve 1.63X and 1.22X throughput speedups in long-context and short-context settings, respectively. gpt-oss-puzzle-88B also delivers throughput speedups of 2.82X on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU. However, because token counts can change with reasoning effort and model variants, per-token throughput (tok/s) and latency (ms/token) do not necessarily lead to end-to-end speedups: a 2X throughput gain is erased if traces grow 2X. Conversely, throughput gains can be spent on more reasoning tokens to improve accuracy; we therefore advocate request-level efficiency metrics that normalize throughput by tokens generated and trace an accuracy--speed frontier across reasoning efforts. We show that gpt-oss-puzzle-88B improves over gpt-oss-120B along the entire frontier, delivering up to 1.29X higher request-level efficiency. Across various benchmarks, gpt-oss-puzzle-88B matches or slightly exceeds the parent on suite-average accuracy across reasoning efforts, with retention ranging from 100.8% (high) to 108.2% (low), showing that post-training architecture search can substantially reduce inference costs without sacrificing quality.
estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

title: Profiling LoRA/QLoRA Fine-Tuning Efficiency on Consumer GPUs: An RTX 4060 Case Study
abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) with parameter-efficient techniques such as LoRA and QLoRA has enabled adaptation of foundation models on modest hardware. Yet the efficiency of such training on consumer-grade GPUs, especially under strict 8 GB VRAM limits, remains underexplored. We present a controlled profiling study of LoRA/QLoRA fine-tuning using the Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct model on a single NVIDIA RTX 4060. Across three representative configurations, we systematically vary batch size, sequence length, optimizer choice (AdamW vs. PagedAdamW), and precision (fp16 vs. bf16). We report throughput (tokens/s), time per 10k tokens, and VRAM footprint, alongside energy estimates derived from GPU board power limits. Our results show that paged optimizers improve throughput by up to 25% (628 tok/s vs. 500 tok/s baseline), while bf16 degrades efficiency relative to fp16. Despite 8 GB constraints, sequence lengths up to 2048 tokens were feasible using parameter-efficient strategies. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic case study of LLM fine- tuning efficiency on consumer GPUs, providing reproducible benchmarks and practical guidelines for resource-constrained researchers and practitioners.
estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

title:
ALISE: Accelerating Large Language Model Serving with Speculative
  Scheduling
abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) represent a revolutionary advancement in the
contemporary landscape of artificial general intelligence (AGI). As exemplified
by ChatGPT, LLM-based applications necessitate minimal response latency and
maximal throughput for inference serving. However, due to the unpredictability
of LLM execution, the first-come-first-serve (FCFS) scheduling policy employed
by current LLM serving systems suffers from head-of-line (HoL) blocking issues
and long job response times.
  In this paper, we propose a new efficient LLM inference serving framework,
named ALISE. The key design paradigm of ALISE is to leverage a novel
speculative scheduler by estimating the execution time for each job and
exploiting such prior knowledge to assign appropriate job priority orders, thus
minimizing potential queuing delays for heterogeneous workloads. Furthermore,
to mitigate the memory overhead of the intermediate key-value (KV) cache, we
employ a priority-based adaptive memory management protocol and
quantization-based compression techniques. Evaluations demonstrate that in
comparison to the state-of-the-art solution vLLM, ALISE improves the throughput
of inference serving by up to 1.8x and 2.1x under the same latency constraint
on the Alpaca and ShareGPT datasets, respectively.
estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

title: Beyond Per-Token Pricing: A Concurrency-Aware Methodology for LLM Infrastructure Cost Estimation
abstract: Every public LLM cost calculator we surveyed treats GPU utilization as a fixed input -- entered by the user, baked in as a preset, or silently assumed at 100% -- never measured against the operator's actual load. We show that this assumption is the dominant source of error: on identical H100 hardware, effective cost spans \0.21 to 15.25 per million output tokens, an underutilization penalty of 2.5-24x across low-to-moderate enterprise loads (1-10 rps) and up to 36.3x near idle -- driven by one operator-controlled variable, offered request rate lambda, which sets in-flight concurrency via Little's Law and which no open-source calculator exposes. Because calculators take utilization as a user-supplied input, any utilization-naive estimate understates true cost by exactly 1/U, systematically mispricing self-hosting -- most severely over-selling it for low-traffic workloads. We propose a measurement methodology that parameterizes the relationship as C_eff = f(H, M, Q, lambda, L), validate it with 42 benchmarks across dense, ultra-sparse MoE, and sparse MoE models, and release vllm-cost-meter, an open-source cost meter that attaches to a live vLLM server and reports real \$/M-tokens against the operator's own traffic. We further show that FP8 quantization benefits the MoE architectures we tested roughly 2.2-2.4x more than the dense model (+69 to +74% vs. +31% peak throughput; n=3, broader validation needed), and our data are consistent with active parameter count, not total model size, being a primary predictor of saturation economics. To rule out single-hardware confounding we repeat the core sweep on A100 80GB PCIe (56 runs): the load-driven spread reproduces at 7.0-11.4x, the active-parameters ordering survives at FP8, and the dense-FP8 advantage inverts on silicon without native FP8 tensor cores -- a hardware-conditional caveat the framework already accommodates.
estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

title: Parallel Scaling Law for Language Models
abstract:
It is commonly believed that scaling language models should commit a
significant space or time cost, by increasing the parameters (parameter
scaling) or output tokens (inference-time scaling). We introduce the third and
more inference-efficient scaling paradigm: increasing the model's parallel
computation during both training and inference time. We apply P diverse and
learnable transformations to the input, execute forward passes of the model in
parallel, and dynamically aggregate the P outputs. This method, namely
parallel scaling (ParScale), scales parallel computation by reusing existing
parameters and can be applied to any model structure, optimization procedure,
data, or task. We theoretically propose a new scaling law and validate it
through large-scale pre-training, which shows that a model with P parallel
streams is similar to scaling the parameters by O(log P) while showing
superior inference efficiency. For example, ParScale can use up to 22times
less memory increase and 6times less latency increase compared to parameter
scaling that achieves the same performance improvement. It can also recycle an
off-the-shelf pre-trained model into a parallelly scaled one by post-training
on a small amount of tokens, further reducing the training budget. The new
scaling law we discovered potentially facilitates the deployment of more
powerful models in low-resource scenarios, and provides an alternative
perspective for the role of computation in machine learning.
estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

title:
SambaNova SN40L: Scaling the AI Memory Wall with Dataflow and
  Composition of Experts
abstract:
Monolithic large language models (LLMs) like GPT-4 have paved the way for
modern generative AI applications. Training, serving, and maintaining
monolithic LLMs at scale, however, remains prohibitively expensive and
challenging. The disproportionate increase in compute-to-memory ratio of modern
AI accelerators have created a memory wall, necessitating new methods to deploy
AI. Composition of Experts (CoE) is an alternative modular approach that lowers
the cost and complexity of training and serving. However, this approach
presents two key challenges when using conventional hardware: (1) without fused
operations, smaller models have lower operational intensity, which makes high
utilization more challenging to achieve; and (2) hosting a large number of
models can be either prohibitively expensive or slow when dynamically switching
between them.
  In this paper, we describe how combining CoE, streaming dataflow, and a
three-tier memory system scales the AI memory wall. We describe Samba-CoE, a
CoE system with 150 experts and a trillion total parameters. We deploy
Samba-CoE on the SambaNova SN40L Reconfigurable Dataflow Unit (RDU) - a
commercial dataflow accelerator architecture that has been co-designed for
enterprise inference and training applications. The chip introduces a new
three-tier memory system with on-chip distributed SRAM, on-package HBM, and
off-package DDR DRAM. A dedicated inter-RDU network enables scaling up and out
over multiple sockets. We demonstrate speedups ranging from 2x to 13x on
various benchmarks running on eight RDU sockets compared with an unfused
baseline. We show that for CoE inference deployments, the 8-socket RDU Node
reduces machine footprint by up to 19x, speeds up model switching time by 15x
to 31x, and achieves an overall speedup of 3.7x over a DGX H100 and 6.6x over a
DGX A100.
estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

title: AI Flow at the Network Edge
abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) and their multimodal variants have led to remarkable progress across various domains, demonstrating impressive capabilities and unprecedented potential. In the era of ubiquitous connectivity, leveraging communication networks to distribute intelligence is a transformative concept, envisioning AI-powered services accessible at the network edge. However, pushing large models from the cloud to resource-constrained environments faces critical challenges. Model inference on low-end devices leads to excessive latency and performance bottlenecks, while raw data transmission over limited bandwidth networks causes high communication overhead. This article presents AI Flow, a framework that streamlines the inference process by jointly leveraging the heterogeneous resources available across devices, edge nodes, and cloud servers, making intelligence flow across networks. To facilitate cooperation among multiple computational nodes, the proposed framework explores a paradigm shift in the design of communication network systems from transmitting information flow to intelligence flow, where the goal of communications is task-oriented and folded into the inference process. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework through an image captioning use case, showcasing the ability to reduce response latency while maintaining high-quality captions. This article serves as a position paper for identifying the motivation, challenges, and principles of AI Flow.
estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

title:
TokenWeave: Efficient Compute-Communication Overlap for Distributed LLM
  Inference
abstract:
Distributed inference of large language models (LLMs) can introduce overheads
of up to 20% even over GPUs connected via high-speed interconnects such as
NVLINK. Multiple techniques have been proposed to mitigate these overheads by
decomposing computations into finer-grained tasks and overlapping communication
with sub-tasks as they complete. However, fine-grained decomposition of a large
computation into many smaller computations on GPUs results in overheads.
Further, the communication itself uses many streaming multiprocessors (SMs),
adding to the overhead.
  We present TokenWeave to address these challenges. TokenWeave proposes a
Token-Splitting technique that divides the tokens in the inference batch into
two approximately equal subsets in a wave-aware manner. The computation of one
subset is then overlapped with the communication of the other. In addition,
TokenWeave optimizes the order of the layer normalization computation with
respect to communication operations and implements a novel fused
AllReduce-RMSNorm kernel carefully leveraging Multimem instruction support
available on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs. These optimizations allow TokenWeave to
perform communication and RMSNorm using only 2-8 SMs. Moreover, our kernel
enables the memory bound RMSNorm to be overlapped with the other batch's
computation, providing additional gains. Our evaluations demonstrate up to 29%
latency gains and up to 26% throughput gains across multiple models and
workloads. In several settings, TokenWeave results in better performance
compared to an equivalent model with all communication removed.
estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

title: Hydra: Phase-Aware Workload Characterization of LLM Inference across Edge SoC Generations, Backends, and Quantization Levels
abstract: Edge LLM deployment is shaped by more than model size and precision: inference backend, hardware platform, memory traffic, and power management all affect latency and efficiency. We present Hydra, a common-schema, phase-aware workload characterization framework for LLM inference on edge SoCs. Hydra instruments HuggingFace Transformers and llama.cpp with a shared per-prompt timing schema and fuses those records with hardware telemetry, enabling a multi-dimensional characterization of performance, system-resource utilization, and efficiency across prefill and decode phases. Using Hydra, we evaluate three consecutive edge System-on-Chip (SoC) generations (AGX Xavier, AGX Orin, and AGX Thor), 13 instruction-tuned LLMs from seven families, five execution formats, and consider input/output-length sensitivity. The resulting artifact contains roughly 107K per-prompt records and is publicly released with Hydra. Our analysis shows that aggregate latency alone hides key deployment effects: backend structure changes where latency is introduced, quantization reduces memory traffic and energy but does not predict power monotonically, and SoC generation changes how utilization and efficiency should be interpreted. By connecting phase-level timing with system-resource utilization and efficiency metrics, Hydra enables reproducible, phase-aware characterization of edge LLM inference. Hydra's source code and the collected per-prompt trace corpus are available open-source at: https://github.com/amirtaherin/hydra
estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

title: AIConfigurator: Lightning-Fast Configuration Optimization for Multi-Framework LLM Serving
abstract: Optimizing Large Language Model (LLM) inference in production systems is increasingly difficult due to dynamic workloads, stringent latency/throughput targets, and a rapidly expanding configuration space. This complexity spans not only distributed parallelism strategies (tensor/pipeline/expert) but also intricate framework-specific runtime parameters such as those concerning the enablement of CUDA graphs, available KV-cache memory fractions, and maximum token capacity, which drastically impact performance. The diversity of modern inference frameworks (e.g., TRT-LLM, vLLM, SGLang), each employing distinct kernels and execution policies, makes manual tuning both framework-specific and computationally prohibitive. We present AIConfigurator, a unified performance-modeling system that enables rapid, framework-agnostic inference configuration search without requiring GPU-based profiling. AIConfigurator combines (1) a methodology that decomposes inference into analytically modelable primitives - GEMM, attention, communication, and memory operations while capturing framework-specific scheduling dynamics; (2) a calibrated kernel-level performance database for these primitives across a wide range of hardware platforms and popular open-weights models (GPT-OSS, Qwen, DeepSeek, LLama, Mistral); and (3) an abstraction layer that automatically resolves optimal launch parameters for the target backend, seamlessly integrating into production-grade orchestration systems. Evaluation on production LLM serving workloads demonstrates that AIConfigurator identifies superior serving configurations that improve performance by up to 40% for dense models (e.g., Qwen3-32B) and 50% for MoE architectures (e.g., DeepSeek-V3), while completing searches within 30 seconds on average. Enabling the rapid exploration of vast design spaces - from cluster topology down to engine specific flags.
estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

title:
Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than
  Scaling Model Parameters
abstract:
Enabling LLMs to improve their outputs by using more test-time computation is
a critical step towards building generally self-improving agents that can
operate on open-ended natural language. In this paper, we study the scaling of
inference-time computation in LLMs, with a focus on answering the question: if
an LLM is allowed to use a fixed but non-trivial amount of inference-time
compute, how much can it improve its performance on a challenging prompt?
Answering this question has implications not only on the achievable performance
of LLMs, but also on the future of LLM pretraining and how one should tradeoff
inference-time and pre-training compute. Despite its importance, little
research attempted to understand the scaling behaviors of various test-time
inference methods. Moreover, current work largely provides negative results for
a number of these strategies. In this work, we analyze two primary mechanisms
to scale test-time computation: (1) searching against dense, process-based
verifier reward models; and (2) updating the model's distribution over a
response adaptively, given the prompt at test time. We find that in both cases,
the effectiveness of different approaches to scaling test-time compute
critically varies depending on the difficulty of the prompt. This observation
motivates applying a "compute-optimal" scaling strategy, which acts to most
effectively allocate test-time compute adaptively per prompt. Using this
compute-optimal strategy, we can improve the efficiency of test-time compute
scaling by more than 4x compared to a best-of-N baseline. Additionally, in a
FLOPs-matched evaluation, we find that on problems where a smaller base model
attains somewhat non-trivial success rates, test-time compute can be used to
outperform a 14x larger model.
estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

title: TokenRouter: Efficient Serving System for Token-Level LLM Routing
abstract: Large language model (LLM) routing distributes inference work across different models, advancing the cost-quality Pareto frontier of LLM serving. While coarse-grained routing at the session or query level has been widely adopted in production systems, recent algorithmic work shows that fine-grained token-level routing can yield substantial efficiency and quality gains. However, efficiently serving token-level routed inference poses significant challenges to existing systems. Built on single-LLM assumptions, current systems suffer from severe step desynchronization and frequent batch admission delays under token-level routing, and they also impose high implementation complexity on developers. To address these challenges, we design TokenRouter, an efficient and developer-friendly serving system for token-level routed LLM inference. TokenRouter follows the principle of request-centric programming, model-centric execution: developers describe routing logic from the perspective of a single request, while the runtime launches a subserver for each LLM and dispatches requests asynchronously. Each subserver employs a delayed-batching scheduler, whose optimal hyperparameters are derived from a mathematical throughput model of the system. Across diverse routing algorithms, workloads, and model pairs, TokenRouter achieves 2.01-64.15x higher decoding throughput than existing systems, substantially advancing the serving efficiency of token-level LLM routing. Our code is available at https://github.com/thu-nics/TokenRouter.
estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

title:
InstInfer: In-Storage Attention Offloading for Cost-Effective
  Long-Context LLM Inference
abstract:
The widespread of Large Language Models (LLMs) marks a significant milestone
in generative AI. Nevertheless, the increasing context length and batch size in
offline LLM inference escalate the memory requirement of the key-value (KV)
cache, which imposes a huge burden on the GPU VRAM, especially for
resource-constraint scenarios (e.g., edge computing and personal devices).
Several cost-effective solutions leverage host memory or SSDs to reduce storage
costs for offline inference scenarios and improve the throughput. Nevertheless,
they suffer from significant performance penalties imposed by intensive KV
cache accesses due to limited PCIe bandwidth. To address these issues, we
propose InstInfer, a novel LLM inference system that offloads the most
performance-critical computation (i.e., attention in decoding phase) and data
(i.e., KV cache) parts to Computational Storage Drives (CSDs), which minimize
the enormous KV transfer overheads. InstInfer designs a dedicated flash-aware
in-storage attention engine with KV cache management mechanisms to exploit the
high internal bandwidths of CSDs instead of being limited by the PCIe
bandwidth. The optimized P2P transmission between GPU and CSDs further reduces
data migration overheads. Experimental results demonstrate that for a 13B model
using an NVIDIA A6000 GPU, InstInfer improves throughput for long-sequence
inference by up to 11.1times, compared to existing SSD-based solutions such
as FlexGen.
estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

title: AgentCgroup: Understanding and Controlling OS Resources of AI Agents
abstract: AI agents are increasingly deployed in multi-tenant cloud environments, where they execute diverse tool calls within sandboxed containers, each call with distinct resource demands and rapid fluctuations. We present a systematic characterization of OS-level resource dynamics in sandboxed AI coding agents, analyzing 144 software engineering tasks from the SWE-rebench benchmark across two LLM models. Our measurements reveal that (1) OS-level execution (tool calls, container and agent initialization) accounts for 56-74% of end-to-end task latency; (2) memory, not CPU, is the concurrency bottleneck; (3) memory spikes are tool-call-driven with a up to 15.4x peak-to-average ratio; and (4) resource demands are highly unpredictable across tasks, runs, and models. Comparing these characteristics against serverless, microservice, and batch workloads, we identify three mismatches in existing resource controls: a granularity mismatch (container-level policies vs. tool-call-level dynamics), a responsiveness mismatch (user-space reaction vs. sub-second unpredictable bursts), and an adaptability mismatch (history-based prediction vs. non-deterministic stateful execution). We propose AgentCgroup, an intent-driven eBPF-based resource controller that exploits agents ability to declare resource needs and reconstruct execution strategies, using hierarchical cgroup structures aligned with tool-call boundaries, in-kernel enforcement via sched_ext and memcg_bpf_ops, and runtime-adaptive policies. Preliminary evaluation demonstrates improved multi-tenant isolation and reduced resource waste. AgentCgroup is open-source at https://github.com/eunomia-bpf/agentcgroup
estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

supplement_records.title: AgentCgroup: Understanding and Controlling OS Resources of AI Agents

title: Shift Parallelism: Low-Latency, High-Throughput LLM Inference for Dynamic Workloads
abstract:
Efficient parallelism is necessary for achieving low-latency, high-throughput inference with large language models (LLMs). Tensor parallelism (TP) is the state-of-the-art method for reducing LLM response latency, however GPU communications reduces combined token throughput. On the other hand, data parallelism (DP) obtains a higher throughput yet is slow in response latency. Best of both worlds does not exist, and it is not possible to combine TP and DP because of the KV cache variance across the parallelisms.
  We notice Sequence Parallelism (SP - Ulysses in training) has similar properties as DP but with KV cache invariance. We adapt SP to inference, and combine it with TP to get the best of both worlds. Our solution: Shift Parallelism.
  Shift Parallelism dynamically switches across TP and SP, and minimizes latency in low traffic without losing throughput in high traffic. The efficient GPU communications of Shift Parallelism yields up to i) 1.51x faster response in interactive workloads and ii) 50% higher throughput in batch workloads, compared to a TP-only solution.
  We evaluate Shift Parallelism with real-world production traces with dynamic traffic patterns as well as synthetic benchmarking patterns across models, context sizes, and arrival rates. All results affirm the same: Shift Parallelism has a better the latency vs. throughput tradeoff than TP or DP, and hence obtains low latency without degrading throughput in dynamic workloads.
estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

title: Cascadia: A Control-Plane-Free Alternative to Hyperconverged AI Infrastructure
abstract: We present Cascadia, a system for serving large language models on fleets of commodity Intel AIPCs using their CPU, integrated-GPU, and NPU resources. Every node embeds ingress, scheduling, and execution; inference requests require no dedicated routing control plane. Nodes join a libp2p QUIC mesh using CA-issued ed25519 admission certificates, gossip signed capabilities, exchange live load over direct peer streams, and route OpenAI-compatible requests to eligible peers. An operator-run certificate authority handles admission and fleet management outside the inference path. Three serving modes share one interface: whole-model execution on one node, load-balanced replicas, and pipeline-sharded chains using the compilation and speculative decoding mechanism of our companion paper. Optional KV-cache mobility reuses compatible conversation prefixes after a routing move, with cold recomputation on a miss. Signed response receipts and hash-chained logs support provenance and audit. A three-node Phi-3.5-mini NPU testbed delivered 3.10x the response throughput of its one-node configuration under ten concurrent requests; a separate four-node deployment recorded 4.06x the throughput of direct single-node serving. Paired latency observations, runtime measurements, and internal functional checks characterize the tested configurations. We compare Cascadia with IBM, Nutanix, VMware, and HPE platforms on deployment footprint, hardware requirements, scheduling, scaling, licensing, and trust, using vendor documentation. The paper repository provides benchmark scripts, curated measurements, and a claim-to-evidence map.
estimate_basis: 20 minute maximum bounded check allocation; not measured runtime

title: Neural Evidence for Implicit Processing of Rhythmic Syntax at Musical Cadences
abstract: Rhythmic syntax forms the temporal structural framework essential for musical meaning and emotion. While crucial for music perception, how rhythmic syntax is processed without direct attentional focus remains unknown. Using EEG, we examined this process by manipulating rhythmic syntactic regularity in cadence, comparing sequences ending on metrically strong positions (regular) and those with syncopated endings (irregular). Participants performed a pitch-detection task irrelevant to syntactic processing. The results showed that syntactic irregular endings failed to elicit a significant early right anterior negativity (ERAN), demonstrating the absence of automatic violation detection. In contrast, these violations robustly evoked a late P600, reflecting conscious structural processing of rhythmic syntax. Moreover, we used a deep learning method to confirm the EEG results and further validate the differential processing of regular and irregular rhythmic syntax in the brain. Our study provides direct neurophysiological evidence for the implicit processing of rhythmic syntactic violations in early and late stages.

title: From Access to Governance: Generative AI Literacy for Extension Professionals and Small Businesses, and a Governance-Aware Design Framework
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has become widespread through user-friendly interfaces that require minimal technical skill, yet rural communities and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) still face a capability gap that low barriers to access do not resolve. This review examines how land-grant universities with Cooperative Extension System and other public institutions in the United States are delivering GenAI literacy education, an area of practice that has grown rapidly since late 2022 but has not been systematically reviewed. Drawing on a structured narrative review of published research, institutional program documentation, and grey literature from 2022 to 2026, the review maps the current landscape of Extension and public-sector GenAI education. We group existing programs into four delivery models: single-session workshops, multi-session series, one-on-one technical consulting, and asynchronous online modules. Hybrid configurations combine these models. Our review then identifies six challenges that cut across programs, which consist of the need for scaffolding, a governance gap between individual acceptance and organizational readiness, cost sensitivity and tool proliferation, a digital literacy paradox, persistent equity exclusions, and the capacity gap within Extension itself. Building on these findings, we recommend a governance-aware design framework organized around four questions of what to teach, how to teach, who teaches, and how to evaluate. The framework considers governance capability as core content rather than an optional addition and offers state Extension systems, funders, and policymakers a structure that can be adapted. The review concludes with a research agenda for longitudinal, organizational, and equity-focused work.

title: Large Language Models in Clinical Decision Support: A Critical Review of Progress, Limitations, and the Path Toward Sustainable Healthcare
abstract: Large language models such as GPT-4, Med-PaLM 2, and BioMedLM are being increasingly applied to clinical decision support tasks including diagnostic reasoning, clinical documentation, medical question answering, and patient-facing health communication, with several studies reporting performance comparable to trained clinicians on structured benchmarks. However, the current pace of adoption has outrun the critical evaluation of whether these models are genuinely safe, equitable, and sustainable for deployment in real-world healthcare environments. This narrative review argues that the existing literature has focused disproportionately on benchmark performance while giving insufficient attention to the conditions required for these models to function as trustworthy long-term clinical tools. Drawing on published evidence across medical informatics, clinical artificial intelligence, and natural language processing, we synthesise model performance across four clinical task areas and examine documented limitations including factual hallucination, demographic bias, and poor generalisability outside controlled settings that are already present in current deployments. We further identify five structural sustainability challenges that obstruct responsible deployment at scale, and propose a corresponding five-pillar framework alongside a priority research agenda for closing the gaps this review identifies. This review contributes a critically grounded perspective to the growing discourse on artificial intelligence for sustainable healthcare, with direct relevance to Sustainable Development Goal 3 (Good Health and Well-Being) and Sustainable Development Goal 10 (Reduced Inequalities), and offers concrete guidance for developing clinical models that are safe, inclusive, and viable across diverse global health contexts.

title: From Human Empathy to AI-Generated Empathic Performance: Conceptual Boundaries and Ethical Risks for Human-Centered AI
abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into everyday communication has complicated the conceptual boundaries of empathy by enabling systems to generate responses that appear emotionally attentive, supportive, and context-sensitive. Through a concept-centered theoretical synthesis of scholarship on human empathy, artificial empathy, human&ndash;AI interaction, and AI ethics, this article distinguishes three analytically distinct phenomena: human empathy, AI-generated empathic performance, and perceived AI empathy. In the present framework, human empathy is organized around four dimensions&mdash;cognitive understanding, affective responsiveness, self&ndash;other differentiation, and communicative expression&mdash;which are used as analytical reference points for comparing the observable capacities and conceptual limits of AI-generated empathic performance. The analysis argues that AI systems can approximate communicative features associated with empathy through emotional and contextual inference, affect-sensitive expression, adaptive response generation, and conversational continuity, but such performance should not be treated as equivalent to the relational and experiential dimensions of human empathy. Perceived AI empathy is shaped by source attribution, interactional context, and user interpretation. The resulting ethical implications concern attributional and relational risks, vulnerability, data and fairness, transparency, accountability, and governance. Operationally, the framework supports separate evaluation of system performance and perceived empathy, disclosure of AI status and inferential limits, communication of uncertainty in emotion inference, calibration of anthropomorphic and relational cues, and pathways to human support in emotionally sensitive or high-stakes contexts.

title: A Novel E-Commerce Search Engine Based on Multimodal Generative AI for Improving Product Accessibility
abstract: E-commerce search engines often fall short in delivering accurate and fair results due to their reliance on keyword matching and bias towards larger companies. This paper introduces a novel search engine architecture that integrates advanced AI techniques to address these limitations. Our approach combines Large Language Models (LLMs) for semantic query understanding and Multimodal LLMs (specifically LLaVA) for extracting detailed information from product images to enrich product descriptions. More specifically, we employ a fine-tuned version of the CLIP model to create a unified embedding of product images and descriptions, storing them in a vector database to enable efficient semantic search. Moreover, we fine-tuned the LLaVA model on e-commerce-specific data, significantly improving its performance in generating accurate product descriptions, which were also added to the vector database. The integration of computer vision (CV) techniques allows for a better interpretation of visual product attributes, while the use of vector databases facilitates rapid and relevant search results. Our system also incorporates a recommendation mechanism that leverages these advanced models to provide wider product recommendations. Our experiments demonstrate substantial improvements: the fine-tuned LLaVA model achieved an 80.57% human evaluation rating compared to 62.89% for the original model. Moreover, the overall search accuracy increased after fine-tuning the system by 25 percent points, from 70% to 95%. Our work promotes a more equitable platform for e-commerce search engines while significantly improving user satisfaction.

title: People as Sensors: An End-to-End Deep Learning Framework for Near-Real-Time Wildfire Detection, Classification, and Geospatial Intelligence from Greek Social Media
abstract: Citizens&rsquo; social media posts can provide rapid, complementary situational information during emerging wildfires, alongside conventional sensing and official reporting. For Greek, no annotated wildfire corpus or end-to-end pipeline existed, and most systems stop at binary detection or depend on geotags. We present an end-to-end Greek-language NLP pipeline, a research prototype that turns keyword-retrieved, unlabeled X posts into a geolocated, near-real-time wildfire map: it detects active fires, types them as wildland, urban, or mixed, resolves toponyms, and clusters reports into incidents. On 3277 manually annotated posts from two fire seasons, the first publicly released, agreement-audited Greek wildfire corpus to our knowledge, fine-tuned transformers reached F2 = 0.911 for detection and macro-F1 = 0.874 for fire type, outperforming classical baselines and, under the tested prompting conditions, two large language models, while being faster and free of API costs. On a chronological hold-out of the unseen 2025 season, detection retains F2 = 0.850 (classification recall 0.907); fire-type classification degrades more (macro-F1 0.769 &plusmn; 0.085). Spatiotemporal toponym disambiguation raised geocoding accuracy from 54.68% to 80.58% (p &lt; 0.001); a repeatability test revealed gazetteer drift. In a retrospective replay of 12 August 2024 posts, it resolved hundreds of reports of an Attica wildfire into one incident cluster, complementing emergency calls.

title: Assurance of Safety-Critical AI-Enabled Capabilities: Integrating Human, Software, and Machine Learning Assurance Paradigms
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enabled systems are now increasingly deployed across safety-critical, mission-critical, and socio-technical domains. Existing engineering disciplines offer mature approaches to human and software assurance; however, AI-enabled systems can exhibit characteristics such as probabilistic behaviour, data dependency, limited explainability, and adaptation that challenge traditional assurance methods. Our research examines assurance precepts across three domains that arguably dominated assurance reforms in capability development during different periods: (1) human assurance, circa 1980 to 2000, (2) software assurance, circa 2000 to 2020, and (3) assurance of AI-enabled systems, emerging since 2020. While software assurance is largely concerned with verifying deterministic behaviour against specified requirements and human assurance focuses on managing variability in socio-technical systems, AI assurance must address systems whose behaviour is learned, probabilistic, and inherently dependent on data. We contribute a set of 20 assurance precepts for safety-critical AI-enabled capabilities. To extend current assurance frameworks, we structured these precepts across four quadrants of assurance activities, responsibilities, and critical questions, and organized them within a novel Dual Assurance Spiral for AI-enabled Capabilities (DAS4AIC). We propose the DAS4AIC to operationalise the 20 AI assurance precepts throughout capability development and sustainment. Further, we demonstrate how classical safety precepts map from human-dominant assurance through software-dominant assurance to the assurance of AI-enabled systems with conceptual validation. Our preliminary evaluation is that some human assurance precepts map more directly to AI-enabled systems than through the intermediate step of software assurance, suggesting that established human assurance concepts may have continuing relevance for AI-enabled capabilities. To our knowledge, this is the first study to align emerging AI-assurance precepts explicitly with the earlier and still overlapping, human-dominant and software-dominant assurance paradigms.

title: Momentum-Based Byzantine-Resilient Non-Convex Stochastic Optimization with Different Batch Sizes Across Different Clients
abstract: In recent years, many studies have focused on the robustness of federated learning (FL) systems against Byzantine attacks. Prior work has shown that integrating stochastic optimization algorithms with momentum can effectively enhance the robustness, particularly in non-convex scenarios. However, most studies assume a fixed batch size across all workers, which may not be suitable for practical deployments. In this study, we investigate the impact of different batch sizes across different clients on Byzantine robustness in FL. Specifically, we propose a weighted aggregation framework (WAggF), which assigns different weights to gradients received from different clients. WAggF can be easily embedded into various aggregation rules to boost Byzantine resilience. We further establish theoretical convergence guarantees for two momentum-based stochastic optimization algorithms&mdash;Byz-WNSGDM and Byz-EF21-WSGDM&mdash;under WAggF. To reduce communication overhead and enable synchronous training, we incorporate a contractive compressor (which encompasses Top-K as a special case) into the stochastic optimization algorithm. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed algorithms consistently improve robustness against a range of Byzantine attacks.

title: Summer Maize Leaf Area Index Estimation Using Approximate Days After Sowing and Dual-Domain Paired-Difference Features
abstract: Residue-soil mixing and reduced spectral sensitivity complicate summer maize leaf area index (LAI) estimation from unmanned aerial vehicle multispectral imagery. We compared full-plot and canopy domains, paired differences, neighborhood statistics, and approximate days after sowing (DAS), calculated from a common reference date. Five input schemes (B0&ndash;B4) and four algorithms were evaluated using 345 samples collected on five dates in one growing season. Spatial validation comprised ten repetitions of five-fold grouped cross-validation, with preprocessing and feature selection restricted to training data. For gradient boosting decision trees, R2 increased from 0.515 for B0 to 0.686 for B3 and 0.846 for B4, whereas RMSE decreased from 0.834 to 0.671 and 0.470. Low-LAI Bias decreased from 0.580 to 0.343 and 0.160. Fixed-capacity controls supported conditional improvements after adding paired differences and neighborhood statistics. Approximate DAS produced the largest sequential RMSE reduction, mainly through between-date adjustment. Time-baseline and training-fold residual analyses distinguish calendar-time adjustment from within-date predictive information. High-LAI underestimation and unseen-date errors delimit application beyond the sampled dates and production-field conditions. Within this defined scope, the framework provides a reproducible comparison of image-domain representations under heterogeneous production conditions.

title: Explainability for Forecasting Task with Close-Up Option
abstract: Although machine learning-based forecasting models often function as opaque black boxes, explainability methods provide the essential tools required to foster trust in deep learning systems, optimize computational resources, and enhance model accuracy. Motivated by this, we propose a model-agnostic, local explainability method specifically designed for forecasting tasks. Our approach employs a hierarchical structure that is generated iteratively. From the outset, a small number of &ldquo;interpretable components&rdquo; that decompose the input are considered. In the inductive step, the methodology enables analysts to examine the data in greater detail, allowing for a deeper exploration of specific subcomponents whenever a higher resolution is required. This framework inherently provides control over computational costs by tuning the branching factor. The resulting explainability tree shares certain, but not all, properties of the explainability values provided by the SHAP-LIME framework; in this regard, we present some theoretical results. Furthermore, numerical experiments provided evidence that explanation coherence is fundamentally maintained between both methods. We explored the utility of this methodology on a real-world short-term load forecasting LSTM encoder&ndash;decoder model.

title: WarfaRisk: A Reproducible, Fairness-Aware Machine Learning Pipeline for Warfarin Dose Prediction (Prototype)
abstract: Warfarin dosing is complicated by wide inter-patient variability driven by genetic, demographic, and pharmacological factors. Although machine learning approaches to dose prediction have been widely studied, published evaluations are frequently affected by analysis-domain data leakage, small held-out sets, and an absence of calibration and fairness assessment across ancestry subgroups. We describe WarfaRisk, a nine-phase open-source machine learning pipeline for warfarin dose prediction evaluated on two public International Warfarin Pharmacogenetics Consortium (IWPC) cohorts (n=6037 and n=1780, the latter a non-independent secondary consistency check) using fixed patient-level splits and a single documented random seed. The pipeline incorporates leakage-free preprocessing, nested clinical and pharmacogenomic feature ablation across nine model architectures, leave-one-ancestry-out portability assessment with a cross-model robustness check, conformal prediction calibration reported at subgroup resolution, and individual-level SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) feature attribution. The nine-architecture ablation results reported here are from the primary cohort, IWPC-6256; the complete two-cohort comparison is reported in a companion evaluation manuscript. A prototype web-based clinical decision support interface integrates dose recommendation, uncertainty quantification, and SHAP explainability with a Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) R4 endpoint. In preliminary evaluation on a single fixed held-out split, Model Agnostic Prediction Interval Estimator (MAPIE) cross-conformal (5-fold CV+) prediction achieves coverage close to its nominal target when measured across each cohort as a whole. When this coverage is instead stratified by ancestry, a different pattern emerges: coverage for African-ancestry patients falls well short, a gap the aggregate number hides, plausibly explained by alleles missing from the standard IWPC genotype panel and supported by independent pharmacogenetic literature, though not directly demonstrated in this dataset. These findings indicate that subgroup-level calibration reporting is necessary, not optional, since its absence can let a model appear well-calibrated in aggregate while failing a specific population in practice.

title: Two-Stage Attention-Based Insertion Policy for the Dynamic Vehicle Routing Problem
abstract: This paper addresses dynamic vehicle routing with online requests, where insertion heuristics follow fixed rules ignoring the effect of each insertion on later requests. It proposes a two-stage attention-based insertion policy: a first stage selects a vehicle, and a second stage an insertion position within its route. Routes and fleet are encoded by attention, and the policy is trained with REINFORCE and a greedy rollout baseline on the final episode cost instead of immediate insertion costs. It is compared with cheapest, nearest and random insertion and with a single-stage policy over all vehicle&ndash;position pairs, on instances with 10 to 120 customers and degrees of dynamism from 10% to 90%. Both learned policies outperform nearest and random insertion and generalize to unseen sizes and degrees of dynamism. When most customers are dynamic on instances with up to 35 customers, the single-stage policy outperforms cheapest insertion by up to 3.1% and the two-stage policy matches it; otherwise, cheapest insertion remains better. The single-stage policy is cheaper in most settings, but the two-stage policy decides up to 2.7 and trains up to 5.7 times faster, for a cost at most 3.6% higher, and becomes cheaper on large, highly dynamic instances.

title: Exploring Romanian Misinformation with GraphRAG: Community-Level Narratives of COVID-19
abstract: Predefined thematic taxonomies can obscure how misinformation narratives emerge, overlap, and change over time. One way to address this limitation is by developing bottom-up data-driven approaches that identify narratives directly from data. We present a pipeline that extracts entities and relations from news articles using GraphRAG, identifies communities using the Leiden algorithm, and uses this information to explore and predict misinformation. We evaluate the pipeline on a set of Romanian COVID-19 pandemic news articles with expert-defined narrative annotations and adapt the extraction prompts to Romanian. Exploratory results show that in this corpus, the graph for fake news is more fragmented and less modular than the graph for real news; it also contains higher proportions of events, disinformation theory, and vaccine entities, whereas the real-news graph contains higher proportions of locations, hospitals, and public health measures. Communities in the combined graph align weakly with the predefined super-narrative labels, indicating that the two representations group articles differently. Furthermore, expert review of similar articles from communities identified within the combined real&ndash;fake graph suggests that an approach based on entity and community may offer a promising avenue for identifying subtle misinformation strategies. Regarding the prediction task, a three-component ensemble that uses graph information achieves 85.86% macro-F1 (95% CI [78.50, 91.27]) and 86.51% accuracy (95% CI [78.57, 91.27]) on classifying articles as fake or true. These point estimates suggest incremental gains over the two-component ensemble without the graph similarity signal, though these gains are not statistically confirmed at this sample size. Together, these exploratory results illustrate the use of GraphRAG as a tool in pipelines that support the exploration and prediction of misinformation.

title: From Anthropomorphism to Trust: Unpacking the Role of Authenticity in Generative AI and Large Language Models&mdash;A Structured Literature Review and Future Research Agenda
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has changed the conditions under which users encounter and evaluate machine-produced communication. In systems based on large language models, conversational output is no longer merely functional; it can be fluent, context-aware, and socially legible, inviting judgments that extend beyond usefulness, accuracy, or efficiency. Yet the literature still tends to treat anthropomorphism, perceived authenticity, and trust as largely separate constructs, without sufficiently explaining how human-like cues become credible in the eyes of users and how this credibility shapes trust. To address this problem, the present structured literature review synthesizes recent research on anthropomorphism, authenticity-related evaluations, and trust in AI-mediated interaction, with particular attention to conversational AI, generative AI, and LLM-based systems. A structured search in the Web of Science Core Collection identified 655 records; after duplicate removal, screening, and eligibility assessment, 96 studies were retained for qualitative synthesis. The analysis identifies several interrelated thematic patterns, including anthropomorphic cues and social presence, authenticity-related mechanisms in AI-mediated communication, trust formation and calibration, boundary conditions, and behavioral responses to conversational AI. On this basis, the review develops an integrative conceptual framework and proposes perceived anthropomorphic authenticity as a review-derived construct for examining how users evaluate human-like AI communication in relation to trust. The study contributes to human&ndash;AI interaction research by clarifying the role of authenticity-related evaluations between anthropomorphic cues and calibrated trust and by identifying conditions under which human-like communication may be associated with trust, skepticism, overreliance, or trust erosion.

title: Machine Learning Prediction of Blood Loss from Arterial Waveform Feature Analysis in a Nonhuman Primate Hemorrhage Model
abstract: Hemorrhage is the leading cause of preventable death in trauma, yet traditional vital signs can fail to detect early blood loss due to physiological compensatory mechanisms. Objective, continuous monitoring of hemorrhage progression remains an unmet clinical need. This study developed and validated a machine learning model of percent estimated blood loss in a nonhuman primate hemorrhage model. Adult male baboons underwent controlled stepwise hemorrhage to approximately 25% blood loss while high-fidelity arterial waveform and blood loss data were captured. Morphological waveform features were extracted, and a Gradient Boosting model was developed using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. A 10 s window with 10 features achieved a mean coefficient of determination of 0.81 and mean absolute error of 2.5%. On three independently held-out subjects, per-subject coefficient of determination ranged from 0.75 to 0.94 while mean absolute error ranged from 1.4% to 3.3%. Notably, percent estimated blood loss detected hemorrhage a median of 8.1 min before sustained blood pressure decline, at approximately 7% blood loss while systolic pressure remained stable. These findings indicate that arterial waveform morphology can enable accurate, continuous blood loss estimation and may provide early warning before hemorrhage becomes detectable through conventional vital sign monitoring in this preclinical model.

title: FA-DGNet: Pseudo-Supervised Difficulty-Aware Learning and Guided Refinement for Colonoscopic Polyp Segmentation
abstract: Colonoscopy is a crucial method for colorectal cancer screening and the early detection of precancerous polyps; however, accurate polyp segmentation is challenged by factors such as indistinct boundaries, minute or flat structures, and regions of high-intensity interference. Given the spatial variability of these challenges, we propose FA-DGNet, a polyp-segmentation model built upon the HarDNet-68 backbone that integrates &ldquo;pseudo-supervised difficulty learning&rdquo; with &ldquo;guided refinement&rdquo; strategies. The model employs a deterministic training objective that incorporates dilated mask boundaries, locally sparse foreground regions, and brightness-inferred areas prone to artifacts, all without requiring additional manual annotations. The learned difficulty response modulates two stages of the decoder via a bounded residual amplification mechanism, while auxiliary supervision is provided by dedicated artifact and edge detection heads. On the Kvasir-SEG dataset, FA-DGNet achieved a mean Dice coefficient of 0.9071 and a mean Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.8508, outperforming the baseline model&rsquo;s metrics of 0.9006 and 0.8418, respectively. Furthermore, cross-dataset transfer experiments and evaluations across five independent test sets confirmed the model&rsquo;s generalization capability and performance stability. Static performance analysis indicates that the model incurs only marginal increases of approximately 0.43% in active parameters and 0.45% in multiply&ndash;accumulate (MAC) operations. Overall, FA-DGNet offers a low-overhead, difficulty-aware optimization strategy, providing a practical solution for colonoscopic polyp segmentation.

title: Cryptanalysis and Improvement of an Image Cryptosystem via Chaotic Synchronization and Artificial Neural Networks in Modified OTP Scheme
abstract: Chaos-based image ciphers may exhibit favorable statistical metrics while retaining a recoverable algebraic structure. We analyze the modified one-time-pad image cryptosystem of Stoycheva et al., which combines static, Chua-system-derived, and neural masks with channel-wise shuffling and XOR. For observations sharing a fixed or reproduced induced state, we prove that each color channel is equivalent to a plaintext-independent permutation followed by an XOR keystream. The trained neural component supplies a mask but does not alter this external structure. Established base-256 position labels recover the complete equivalent mapping with four chosen-plaintext queries for a 512-by-512 image; known-plaintext, chosen-ciphertext, differential, and black-box analyses are evaluated under explicitly stated access conditions. Under the same state, a one-byte plaintext difference changes exactly one ciphertext byte. We also specify a redesign that renews the three key components per image and couples cross-channel routing and masking to preceding ciphertext bytes. Its inverse is proved correct. Across 15 image&ndash;function trials, decryption was byte exact. Advancing the image counter changed 99.603907% of ciphertext bytes for the same image, and none of eight tested input pairs satisfied the fixed permutation&ndash;XOR affine identity. These results identify the state condition required by the recovery procedures and characterize the tested behavior of the redesigned image transformation.

title: When Does Representation Learning Help Attack-Path Forecasting? A Controlled Multi-Cloud Study with CAPTURE-MC
abstract: Cloud defenders increasingly want to anticipate an attacker&rsquo;s next move, not merely detect the last one. We study attack-path forecasting in multi-cloud environments: given the partial trace of an in-progress campaign, predict the next ATT&amp;CK technique. We present CAPTURE-MC, a heterogeneous temporal-graph model that encodes cross-provider telemetry and forecasts the next technique under a transition prior, and we release MC-PathBench, a synthetic but structurally faithful benchmark with four leakage-controlled generalization splits (temporal, cross-cloud, unseen-composition, and campaign hold-out). Our central contribution is an honest, carefully controlled account of when learned temporal-graph representations help and when they do not. We find that the technique-transition structure is a very strong predictor: when the attacker&rsquo;s current technique is known, a first-order Markov model and a uniform-over-allowed-transitions rule match or exceed CAPTURE-MC and a temporal-graph network, so the deep models add little in that idealized regime. The picture reverses in the realistic regime where the current technique must be inferred: as current-technique certainty degrades, the structural baselines, indexed entirely by it, collapse toward chance, whereas CAPTURE-MC degrades gracefully and nearly doubles their accuracy when the current technique is unknown. CAPTURE-MC is likewise robust to a substantially corrupted transition prior (missing, spurious, or misdirected edges). We also report, transparently, where CAPTURE-MC does not help: gradient-boosted trees remain the best per-event and campaign-level detectors; next-entity and time-to-transition prediction are at chance for every model; and the conformal layer, while achieving coverage, yields prediction sets larger than the list of allowed successors and so is not an efficiency gain. The prior is estimated only from training data, never the generator&rsquo;s graph, which removes a leakage path present in an earlier version of this work and changes several conclusions. The practical lesson for predictive cloud defense is that structural baselines are strong and must be reported, and that the value of representation learning appears precisely where structural assumptions break down.

title: Assessing Trustworthiness in LLMs-Assisted Literature Review: A Case Study of Multimodal Machine Learning in Medicine
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used to support the structured extraction of methodological evidence from scientific literature and to build reviews and surveys. However, their use for scientific evidence extraction raises methodological questions concerning the consistency, correctness, and traceability of the extracted information. To address these aspects, this study assesses the trustworthiness of an LLM-assisted framework for structured methodological evidence extraction. A large-scale full-text corpus of multimodal machine learning in medicine, constructed through a structured literature search and automated open-access full-text retrieval, constitutes a case study for the evaluation. In this study, trustworthiness is operationalised through three complementary dimensions: extraction consistency, correctness, and traceability. The proposed pipeline was applied to 1371open-access full-text articles focused on multimodal machine learning in medicine. These articles were independently analysed using two locally deployed open-weight Large Language Models, Qwen and Gemma 3, through the same constrained prompt and predefined JSON schema. The extraction process was constrained through explicit anti-inference rules, while each structured item was linked to source-level textual evidence to support traceability and subsequent inspection. For selected research questions, extraction consistency was assessed through human inter-annotator agreement, whereas correctness was evaluated against an adjudicated human reference. Additional error analyses examined omissions, negative and Not specified outputs, while a targeted analysis conducted on a restricted subset of articles with Calibration-positive predictions examined the availability, textual fidelity, and methodological relevance of the associated source-linked evidence. Resultsare twofold: (i) methodologically, extraction reliability varied across tasks, with finer-grained categories showing lower positive recovery and more omissions; cross-model agreement alone was not sufficient to establish correctness; (ii) in the application case study, both models identified broadly consistent patterns across the analysed corpus, while datasets, fusion strategies, and reliability-oriented methods were frequently assigned to the Not specified category. Overall, the findings support the use of LLM-assisted extraction for large-scale methodological mapping, while highlighting the value of explicit assessment and human validation for interpreting model outputs.

title: A Variational Neural-Field Interpretation of the Stereo-CeNN Architecture in Light of Disparity-Tuned Cortical Organization
abstract: Stereoscopic vision relies on the ability of the visual system to estimate binocular disparity across the visual field. In computational models, stereo matching can be represented through multiple candidate disparity hypotheses defined over retinotopic position. In this work, we reinterpret the Stereo Cellular Neural Network, here referred to as Stereo-CeNN, within a continuous variational framework and introduce a neural-field representation defined over the joint domain of retinotopic position and disparity. In this interpretation, the discrete activities of the Stereo-CeNN are regarded as samples of a continuous activity field r(x,&nbsp;d,&nbsp;t), where different disparity layers correspond to populations tuned to different disparity preferences. The binocular input drives these populations according to local matching evidence, while spatial interactions within each disparity channel promote coherent activity across neighboring retinotopic locations. The final disparity estimate is obtained, consistently with the original Stereo-CeNN architecture, by selecting the disparity channel with the largest steady-state response at each retinotopic position. We show that the layer-wise organization and local spatial dynamics of the Stereo-CeNN admit a continuous neural-field counterpart, establishing an explicit structural and variational correspondence between the discrete retinotopy&ndash;disparity lattice and a population-level representation of stereopsis. This formulation provides a conceptual bridge between the independently developed Stereo-CeNN architecture and the mesoscale organization of disparity-selective populations observed in visual cortex, without implying a one-to-one anatomical or physiological correspondence. Because Cellular Neural Networks are locally connected dynamical systems originally conceived for analog and mixed-signal VLSI implementation, the same organization is also compatible with general neuromorphic principles of local, parallel, and distributed computation.

title: Impact of Class Imbalance Correction on Biological Feature Selection in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma Methylation Data
abstract: Class imbalance is common in biomedical machine learning, yet imbalance-correction strategies are typically evaluated using predictive performance rather than their effects on biological interpretation. We evaluated six resampling methods: Random Oversampling (ROS), Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE), Adaptive Synthetic Sampling (ADASYN), Random Undersampling (RUS), ClusterCentroids, and AllKNN (All K-Nearest Neighbors), together with a no-resampling baseline, using DNA methylation data from The Cancer Genome Atlas Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cohort. The analysis included 485,578 CpG markers of which 406,807 were retained after quality-control filtering. A continuous feature-ranking framework merging Random Forest importance and ANOVA F-statistics was applied across repeated runs. Biological relevance was evaluated through hypergeometric enrichment against a curated PDAC gene set and preranked Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) using 309 Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways. All seven analysis strategies produced significant enrichment for literature-supported pancreatic cancer-associated genes, with hypergeometric p-values ranging from 3.34&times;10&minus;16 to 1.28&times;10&minus;7. SMOTE recovered the largest absolute number of PDAC-associated genes (141 of 13,827 selected genes), whereas RUS achieved the greatest fold enrichment (2.17-fold; 88 observed versus 40.61 expected). Notably, the no-resampling baseline remained highly competitive, recovering 112 PDAC-associated genes with 1.86-fold enrichment and a p-value of 5.27&times;10&minus;14, indicating that resampling was not necessary to recover biologically relevant features under the evaluated feature-ranking framework. Across methods, 169&ndash;234 of the 309 tested KEGG pathways were significant at false discovery rate &le;0.05. ClusterCentroids produced the largest number of significant pathways (234), followed by the no-resampling baseline (225) and RUS (223). Seven to nine predefined PDAC-focused pathways were recovered per method, with RUS and ClusterCentroids recovering all nine. Core pathways consistently identified across all methods included MAPK, PI3K&ndash;Akt, TGF-&beta;, Notch, Hedgehog, focal adhesion, and cell-cycle signaling. These findings show that resampling strategies produce distinct trade-offs between biomarker coverage, biological specificity, and pathway breadth, supporting biologically informed evaluation rather than selection of a single universally optimal imbalance-correction method.

title: DP-FDT: The Drug Pair-Based Fuzzy Decision Tree for Accurate Drug Combination Prediction
abstract: This paper presents a novel algorithm, the Drug Pair-based Fuzzy Decision Tree (DP-FDT), designed to improve classification performance on imbalanced drug combination datasets. Unlike traditional decision trees, the DP-FDT integrates drug combination feature pairs into its feature selection and node construction processes to better capture the underlying relationships between features from different drugs. The algorithm employs a fuzzy splitting rule that allows samples to be assigned to both child nodes with certain probabilities, thereby enhancing the model&rsquo;s fault tolerance. In addition, logistic regression classifiers are incorporated at impure leaf nodes to provide an additional means of separating samples that cannot be perfectly partitioned. Experimental results on two cell line datasets (A375 and A549) demonstrate that the DP-FDT achieves superior performance, particularly in terms of AUC and F1 score, compared with several state-of-the-art oblique decision trees and a deep learning baseline. It also improves recall for minority classes. Ablation studies confirm the positive contributions of its key components. Furthermore, a preliminary bioinformatics analysis provides insights into the biological processes associated with the most influential features identified by the model. Overall, the DP-FDT offers an effective and interpretable approach for analyzing complex drug combination data.

title: AI-Generated Text Detection via Structural and Semantic Entropy Optimization with Adversarial Learning
abstract: AI-generated text detectors often achieve high in-domain accuracy but remain sensitive to changes in domain, generator, and writing style. This limitation partly arises because conventional detectors rely predominantly on latent language-model representations and fixed decision boundaries, without explicitly characterizing sample-level structural and semantic variation. We introduce S2E-AL, an end-to-end score-aware structure&ndash;semantic entropy adversarial learning framework for AI-generated text detection. S2E-AL encodes local dependency, global contextual, and semantic entropy features into a structure&ndash;semantic representation. A gradient-reversal source classifier discourages this representation from retaining source-specific information, while a score-aware threshold estimator conditions on both the entropy representation and a detached base-detector logit to produce a sample-specific logit adjustment. The adjusted logit is used to estimate the final probability that a text is AI-generated. Across HC3, HC3_Plus, LLMTrace, RAID, and XSum, the score-aware model achieved a macro Accuracy of 90.90% and a macro F1-score of 91.42%. Its performance remained lower on XSum, indicating that substantial domain and stylistic shifts remain challenging. These results suggest that jointly modeling structure&ndash;semantic variation and detector confidence can improve the overall performance&ndash;stability trade-off of AI-generated text detection across heterogeneous test distributions.

title: Stream Reduction in Multi-Stream Graph Convolutional Networks: A Non-Inferiority Study for Skeleton-Based Action Recognition
abstract: Multi-stream graph convolutional networks improve skeleton action recognition by combining representations, but each branch adds inference cost. We evaluate one fixed stream-removal operating point in a CTR-GCN pipeline using a paired non-inferiority protocol on NTU RGB+D 120. A temporal configuration reduced source-frame entries requested from the skeleton store by 53.52%, but lost 3.191 percentage points of accuracy and provided no latency saving after reopening the data mapping. A three-stream configuration then omitted bone motion while retaining 64 temporal positions. Historical RTX 4090 measurements at batch size one, using development checkpoints, showed 24.30&ndash;24.94% lower latency. After development confirmation, the fixed pair was trained on 54,468 examples and evaluated on 59,477 cross-setup test examples. Overall accuracy was 89.1050% for four streams and 89.0277% for three streams; paired setup-bootstrap lower bounds exceeded all three prespecified non-inferiority margins. Stream removal introduced 605 errors and corrected 559, while predicted labels changed for 1778 examples. Thus, a net loss of 46 correct decisions concealed broader redistribution. Recall decreased for 61 of 120 actions. These findings support assessing a branch by its contribution to the complete system, measured cost, and explicit quality tolerances. They do not imply preservation of every action. A separate CPU experiment with the final checkpoints measured 24.67% mean latency saving across three processes on one host. The contribution is a controlled empirical assessment, not a new architecture.

title: Generative AI Literacy and Multidimensional AI Anxiety in Creative Higher Education
abstract: Engagement with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) involves practical literacy as well as learning, professional, sociotechnical, and configuration concerns. This mixed-methods study examined whether these responses were differentiated among Chinese arts-university students.
