title: ProtocolNerd: An Interactive AI Research Assistant for Scientific Protocol Discovery
abstract: A search for a suitable experimental protocol using keywords may not lead to the most appropriate protocol, because the keywords may not include exactly the right terms. ProtocolNerd is a web-based interactive assistant that helps biologists and chemists (so far) find relevant protocols by describing their experiment in plain English and then answering a few follow-up questions. Through these domain-specific questions, users optionally provide additional details about the experiment, such as the organism, sample type, technique, and experimental readout. The system uses these answers to build a profile describing the experiment. For biologists, the system then (i) searches Protocols.io for relevant protocols using TF-IDF (term frequency&ndash;inverse document frequency) keyword matching and embedding-based semantic search, and (ii) queries PubMed with a reformulated version of the request to retrieve related research papers. For chemists, the system searches Europe PMC and PubMed. ProtocolNerd ranks the retrieved protocols and papers based on how well they match the researcher&rsquo;s intent and explains why each result may be relevant. We have evaluated ProtocolNerd on molecular biology queries with a citation-grounded benchmark of 100 papers, each of which cites a particular protocol in its Methods section. Using a short automatically (large language model)-generated query on each such paper&rsquo;s abstract, ProtocolNerd placed the confirmed protocol within its top 10 results 46% of the time. A non-parametric paired test shows that this was significantly better than two strong baselines. On the same benchmark it also found the protocol significantly more often than three general AI research assistants, Elicit (20%), Consensus (8%), and Perplexity (5%). These results suggest that combining interactive profiling, multiple retrieval methods, re-ranking, and explainability can significantly improve protocol discovery for scientific research. When applied to chemistry, ProtocolNerd found 31% of the protocols (or their equivalents) using Europe PMC alone and 45% when including PubMed.

title: Platonic Projection Structures-Based Information Dynamics (PPS-ID): Recursive Transformation of Observable Information
abstract: In recursive learning, model outputs can be reused in subsequent training, linking successive models through the reuse and transformation of observable information. Assessing these processes requires distinguishing changes in observable states from the preservation of task-relevant properties. We introduce PPS-Based Information Dynamics (PPS-ID), a framework connecting the observability perspective of Platonic Projection Structures with trajectory-based evaluation of repeated learning. PPS-ID separates latent-to-observable mappings from training-state transitions and evaluates observable discrepancies, task-dependent directional variation, and example-level correctness histories. Standard factorization conditions specify when the chosen observations admit a closed transition, while decision-margin conditions relate changes in prediction probabilities to preservation of classification decisions. Experiments with CIFAR-10 and sentiment classification using Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) illustrate three distinctions: local similarity can coexist with departure from an initial state; accuracy decline can coexist with lower expected calibration error and higher prediction entropy; and endpoint improvement can coexist with intermediate losses. In five-generation CIFAR-10 distillation across five seeds, fixed-teacher final accuracy exceeds recursive final accuracy by a mean of 1.542 percentage points under soft-only supervision. Mixing ground-truth and soft-target supervision reverses this ranking and raises mean recursive final accuracy from 70.672% to 73.910%. On the binary Stanford Sentiment Treebank task (SST-2) and IMDb, BERT experiments yield dataset- and seed-dependent endpoint rankings; first-generation branch differences limit causal attribution to teacher replacement. PPS-ID provides a common evaluation structure for examining how observable information changes and which task-relevant properties are preserved along a learning trajectory. The results show how supervision regime, reference choice, and intermediate variation affect the interpretation of repeated learning.

title: Semantic Modelling of Ancient Sources Using Ontologies
abstract: Ancient literary evidence is commonly dispersed across works, editions, and citation systems, making passage-level thematic retrieval and aggregation difficult. This study presents SourceArchiveOnto, a lightweight application ontology for representing ancient literary works and their passages together with authorship, citation structure, subject, genre, chronology, and selected geographic metadata. The ontology was developed from explicit requirements and competency questions and reuses established Semantic Web vocabularies where their published semantics match the intended relations; locally defined terms are used where no suitable reusable term was identified. A populated proof-of-concept dataset concerning Western Locris demonstrates the model&rsquo;s use rather than attempting comprehensive coverage of the region or of ancient literature. Evaluation combines dataset statistics, competency-question-driven SPARQL queries, logical consistency checking, and inspection of representative instances. The results show that the schema supports reproducible passage-level retrieval and corpus description across the represented works. The evaluation does not establish cross-regional generalizability, large-scale performance, or comprehensive modelling of provenance, manuscript transmission, and competing interpretations; these remain subjects for future extensions and external validation.

title: One-Sided Residual Certificates for Exact Quantized Image Retrieval
abstract: Exact-score retrieval returns the same ordered top-k and numerical scores as a specified exhaustive computation. Quantized vectors can screen candidates, but their approximation errors require safe upper bounds. We study a one-sided residual certificate, denoted OARC+, which stores the positive-part residual norm for nonnegative queries, replacing the full residual norm at identical payload. The inequality is a direct consequence of Cauchy&ndash;Schwarz; the contribution is its single-scalar specialization, exact-score integration, and controlled resource comparison. Exploratory experiments on 900 Digits gallery items and 357 queries reduced mean refinements by 22.05% for pixels and 16.49% for histograms of oriented gradients (HOG). A revision-stage 4K Large Scale Dataset and Benchmark (4KLSDB) transfer evaluation used 129,484 gallery images and 2000 validation queries, with reported reductions of 46.46% for HOG and 48.71% for HOG combined with hue, saturation, and value histograms (HOG+HSV). The test split remains unused. We characterize when tighter bounds cross the stopping threshold and model the cost needed for refinement savings to offset scanning and sorting. Signed queries require a different certificate, and cached exhaustive scoring was faster on Digits. The evidence concerns certificate selectivity under fixed representations; large-gallery latency, physical input/output (I/O) savings, and confirmatory generalization remain unestablished.

title: HallucinationNerd: A Framework and Tool to Detect Hallucinations and Unsupported Claims
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), agentic systems, and human authors produce text with inline citations, but the cited sources do not always support the claims attributed to them. We present HallucinationNerd, a modular citation-verification engine that decomposes text into atomic claims, retrieves relevant passages from each cited source, and determines whether the source supports the claim. In addition, HallucinationNerd identifies claims that carry no citation and searches user-approved databases to find or refute supporting evidence for them. The system handles five common citation formats, operates on PDFs, web pages, and plain text, and produces per-claim verdicts with evidence pointers. The underlying algorithm mixes parsing (to identify claim&ndash;citation pairs), overlapped chunking, stopword elimination, and AI-based semantic comparison. In head-to-head comparison on the same data, HallucinationNerd substantially outperforms (by about 20% in F1 score) state-of-the-art systems on accuracy and precision on a benchmark built from research papers. HallucinationNerd can also be used to verify the output of other AI systems. For example, we audited a set of outputs of Scholar GPT, a publicly available scholarly research agent. In that sample at least, its citations were faithful to the cited sources.

title: SPARE-RAG: Evidence Repair and Verification-Guided Sequential Neural Pruning for Multi-Hop RAG
abstract: Multi-hop RAG requires complementary facts from multiple documents to form a complete evidence chain. Relevance-based passage selection can miss bridging evidence, while adding more passages can introduce redundancy and distractors. Context compression reduces input length but does not, by itself, establish that the remaining evidence supports all required reasoning steps. We propose SPARE-RAG, which combines evidence repair with verification-guided sequential neural pruning. The key insight is to first repair missing support and then assess each proposed deletion by its effect on the remaining evidence set. Within a fixed candidate pool, the framework first supplements missing support, then proposes passage deletions and checks the remaining evidence before accepting or rejecting each proposed deletion. Experiments on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue with frozen Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct show that SPARE-RAG consistently outperforms the compared methods in answer and evidence quality, achieving Answer F1 scores of 70.27, 52.49, and 35.68, respectively. These results demonstrate that combining evidence repair with verified sequential pruning improves both evidence quality and downstream answer generation.

title: Cryptanalysis and Improved Image Cryptosystem via Chaos and Convolutional Neural Network
abstract: Chaos-based image encryption schemes are often motivated by the apparent randomness of chaotic sequences and by the nonlinear processing capability of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). However, these properties alone do not guarantee cryptographic security. In this work, we present a systematic cryptanalysis of an image-encryption framework combining Logistic-map dynamics, pixel permutation, XOR masking, CNN-based processing, image hiding, and wavelet-domain operations. Under the fixed-state condition considered in our analysis, the reversible encryption core can be reduced to c=&Pi;(p)&oplus;s, where &Pi; is a plaintext-independent permutation and s is a fixed byte-wise mask. The effective secret is therefore characterized by the equivalent pair (&Pi;,s), rather than by the nominal parameters of the underlying chaotic map. Based on this structural reduction, we derive mask-cancellation and differential relations and develop five complementary cryptanalytic methods: chosen-plaintext, known-plaintext, chosen-ciphertext, differential, and model-class black-box attacks. The chosen-plaintext attack recovers the XOR mask from an all-zero query and determines the permutation using position-labelled inputs. The known-plaintext attack constructs cross-sample XOR fingerprints to progressively identify permutation positions when the available plaintexts provide sufficient diversity. The chosen-ciphertext and differential attacks recover the inverse mapping or eliminate the fixed mask through carefully designed query pairs. The black-box attack further uses multi-byte coordinate encoding to identify the complete fixed input&ndash;output transformation without prior knowledge of the block structure. These attacks do not require recovery of the Logistic-map parameters; instead, they directly reconstruct the equivalent transformation required to decrypt ciphertexts generated under the same induced state. In addition, for the explicitly linear fixed-convolution component of the target framework, we perform a separate conditional impulse-response experiment to recover its effective convolution kernel. Experiments on 128&times;128 grayscale images with 16&times;16 blocks demonstrate exact byte-level plaintext recovery for the analyzed fixed-state reversible core, while also showing that known-plaintext recovery depends on sample diversity. The results indicate that reusable and separable permutation&ndash;mask structures remain vulnerable even when embedded in chaos- and CNN-assisted image-processing pipelines, motivating per-image state diversification and stronger key-dependent coupling between permutation and diffusion.

title: Relational Narrative Historiography: A Higher-Order Framework for Representing Competing Historical Narratives
abstract: This paper presents Relational Narrative Historiography (RNH) as a framework paper and testable research hypothesis, not as an empirical study. Historical accounts of the same event frequently diverge across archives, languages, and interpretive communities&mdash;a challenge that extends to any domain where reports conflict or facts remain disputed. Conventional knowledge graphs and Large Language Models may favour frequently represented or dominant accounts, potentially reducing the visibility of minority perspectives and of the uncertainty inherent in contested information. This paper proposes that narratives&mdash;or more generally, contested information bundles&mdash;can be represented as higher-order objects that bind events, claims, actors, sources, locations, temporal anchors, interpretive frames, and internal relations. We introduce Relational Narrative Historiography (RNH), a hypergraph-based framework in which narratives are first-class objects. Unlike pairwise graph models, which represent a narrative through separate narrative nodes and edges, hypergraphs can keep the membership of a narrative explicit and represent higher-order relationships as a single structure. The framework uses three epistemic constructs: Epistemic Weight (the strength of evidence supporting a narrative), Divergence (the quantitative distance between narratives), and Uncertainty (what remains unresolved). We describe the conceptual architecture and mathematical formulation, illustrate the calculations with a numerical example based on semantic similarity, and outline an evaluation protocol. All numerical values presented in the worked example are illustrative and are not derived from any expert-annotated real-world dataset. RNH is proposed as a framework and testable research hypothesis, but its validity still needs to be examined empirically in digital humanities, AI, and knowledge representation.

title: Thermal-Aware Generative Adversarial Augmentation for Small-Sample Induction-Motor Fault Detection Using Infrared Thermography
abstract: Fault diagnosis in induction motors is challenging when only a limited number of labeled infrared thermal images are available for training. Effective small-sample augmentation requires generated images to preserve class-related appearance patterns as well as visual realism. To address this challenge, a thermal-aware generative adversarial network (TA-GAN) is proposed for induction-motor fault diagnosis using pseudo-colour infrared images. An adaptive attention module combines feature intensity and Sobel-gradient information to emphasize component&ndash;state-related thermal patterns. A dual-branch critic jointly evaluates global and attention-weighted features, while an appearance-consistency loss constrains bright-region intensity, gradient structure, and spatial position during generation. The trained generator augments the limited real samples, and the combined dataset is used to train a lightweight classifier. Experiments on acquisition-batch-separated data partitions show improved classification performance over the evaluated real-only baselines under matched classifier-training budgets. The complete framework performs best among the evaluated component and individual-loss configurations. Generated-sample evaluation further indicates improved appearance similarity to real training images compared with a basic conditional GAN, while evaluation on a different motor provides additional evidence of transfer under the tested conditions. Image generation is performed offline, allowing the deployed system to retain the lightweight MobileNetV4 classifier architecture.

title: Adapting Whisper to Karakalpak: Full, Layer-Selective, and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Low-Resource Speech Recognition
abstract: Building dependable automatic speech recognition (ASR) for Karakalpak is hindered by the scarcity of transcribed speech. Whisper handles many languages well, but without adaptation its Karakalpak transcripts remain unreliable, largely because the language combines agglutinative morphology with a Latin alphabet containing letters absent from most other orthographies. Following recent Whisper fine-tuning protocols, we adapt Whisper Large-v2 on the authors&rsquo; openly released Karakalpak Speech Corpus and compare full fine-tuning, layer-selective fine-tuning, and lightweight modules (bottleneck adapters and low-rank adaptation, LoRA) in an otherwise frozen network. On a speaker-independent test set, full fine-tuning reduces the word error rate (WER) from 37.70% to 13.53% and the character error rate from 15.40% to 5.42%. Freezing the lower 13 encoder layers gives comparable accuracy (13.39% WER), and adapters in the upper encoder layers and the decoder reach 15.59% WER with only 5.9M trainable parameters. Substituted special letters remain the most frequent error type. Full fine-tuning raises WER on closely related Kazakh and Uzbek by 4.6 and 6.6 percentage points, whereas adapters and LoRA largely preserve multilingual accuracy. The results provide a reproducible reference point for Karakalpak ASR that may later serve applications in education, public administration, accessibility, and digital language preservation.

title: Data Transformation and Scaling Methods for Zero-Inflated Sparse Data Analysis
abstract: Zero-inflated sparse count data are common in text analytics, where keyword frequencies contain many zeros and highly skewed positive values. This study proposes a systematic model-specific framework that treats predictor transformation and scaling as explicit modeling factors and evaluates their effects across statistically different count and machine-learning models. Raw, log, square root, and binary transformations are combined with no scaling, standard scaling, and maximum-absolute scaling. The resulting pipelines are evaluated using ridge regression, random forest, negative binomial regression, zero-inflated negative binomial regression, and a two-part negative binomial model on extended reality patent keyword data with varying levels of sparsity. The results show that preprocessing effects differ substantially across model classes. Random Forest showed strong predictive performance under the full predictor setting and required little preprocessing, whereas continuous transformations provided modest improvements for Ridge and two-part NB models. Binary transformation with standard scaling substantially improves the predictive stability of negative binomial and zero-inflated negative binomial models by reducing extreme errors and convergence problems. These findings demonstrate that transformation and scaling should be selected jointly with the prediction model, response sparsity, and analytical objective rather than applied as universal preprocessing steps.

title: Are Learner Personas Warranted? A Fuzzy-Clustering Diagnostic of Level and Shape in Learning-Attitude Profiles
abstract: Designers may use learner personas to plan different content, feedback, or support for groups of students, but a clustering result alone does not establish that these groups represent distinct learner types. Whether such a categorical structure exists in the data deriving those personas is rarely tested. This paper therefore proposes an uncertainty-aware fuzzy learner-modeling framework in which fuzzy partitioning serves as a diagnostic instrument rather than as a means of generating learner types. The study applies the framework to six learning-attitude constructs measured in three undergraduate cohorts taking AI-supported courses at a Taiwanese university of technology (N = 107; 90 retained after response-quality screening). It estimates fuzzy c-means partitions for two to five clusters at the primary fuzzifier value m = 2.0, with the two- and three-cluster solutions re-estimated at m = 1.5 and m = 2.5 as sensitivity checks. The two-cluster solution is stable (adjusted Rand index = 0.891) and reasonably crisp, yet all centroids differ only in overall level. Elevation accounts for 71.0% of the standardized variance, clustering the shape component alone is uninformative, and the structural criterion consequently fails. The construct with the lowest within-person centered standardized score relates to cohort (Monte Carlo p = 0.009), but no statistically significant association with modal cluster membership is detected (Monte Carlo p = 0.240). These findings insufficiently support distinct configural learner personas in this sample, using this instrument and these six constructs. The paper contributes to debates on person-centered learner modeling by specifying a diagnostic sequence that examines profile shape before interpreting stable, concentrated fuzzy partitions as learner personas. The support-priority vector remains an exploratory description of within-person score contrasts; its instructional value has not been tested.

title: Toward Explainable AI for Acute Kidney Injury Prediction in the ICU: Transparent Development, Internal Validation, and Robustness Auditing of Machine Learning Models
abstract: Background/Objectives: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is common in critical care, yet predictive artificial intelligence studies often differ in outcome definitions, validation, calibration, and interpretability. We developed and internally validated machine learning models for newly observed serum-creatinine-defined AKI after a fixed 24 h ICU landmark and then audited how stable the selected model was to clinically important observation and timing choices. Methods: Using MIMIC-IV v3.1, we retained one first ICU stay per adult patient, required adequate pre-landmark creatinine observation, excluded coded end-stage kidney disease, documented dialysis before the landmark, and observed AKI by the landmark. The outcome was a new creatinine rise within the next 48 h using KDIGO-aligned creatinine change thresholds, with follow-up truncated at ICU exit, hospital discharge, or death. The ascertainable cohort (n = 15,231) was split 60%/15%/10%/15% into training, calibration, validation, and test sets. Logistic regression, random forests, and histogram gradient boosting were calibrated with a separate calibration set; thresholds were fixed on validation data to target at least 80% sensitivity. The test set was evaluated once. A later post hoc audit reused frozen test risks without retraining. Results: Histogram gradient boosting was selected by validation average precision. In 2286 test patients (664 events; 29.0%), AUROC was 0.726 (95% CI, 0.701&ndash;0.749), average precision 0.523 (0.478&ndash;0.565), and Brier score 0.179 (0.171&ndash;0.187). At the fixed threshold, sensitivity was 78.5%, specificity 52.2%, positive predictive value 40.2%, and false alerts 33.9 per 100 patients. Mean predicted risk was 0.290 versus an observed event fraction of 0.290; calibration intercept and slope were 0.023 and 1.022. The AUROC difference versus full logistic regression was +0.0197 (95% CI, 0.00235&ndash;0.03571). Frozen-model sensitivity analyses produced AUROCs from 0.697 to 0.733 in most observation and measurement subsets. However, 15,900 otherwise eligible patients had indeterminate outcomes and showed substantially shorter follow-up and fewer post-landmark creatinine measurements. Conclusions: The selected model showed moderate discrimination and close aggregate calibration under internal validation. Discrimination was similar across several post hoc subsets, although calibration and threshold-based performance changed under stricter observation rules. The main limitation was observation-dependent outcome ascertainment. This work supports transparent model auditing as part of trustworthy AI evaluation, but it does not provide external validation, patient-level explanation validation, or evidence of clinical benefit. Multicenter temporal validation and prospectively defined observation rules are needed before clinical use.

title: Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Japanese Voice Cloning to Dub Chinese Short Dramas: A Four-System Benchmark with Human Evaluation
abstract: Chinese short-form dramas (duanju) drive a growing demand for automated Japanese dubbing that preserves each character&rsquo;s voice. The decisive component is zero-shot cross-lingual voice cloning: synthesising Japanese speech from a short Chinese reference clip. We benchmark four neural text-to-speech systems&mdash;GPT-SoVITS v3, F5-TTS, CosyVoice2-0.5B, and the non-cloning commercial baseline EdgeTTS&mdash;on an annotated short-drama corpus (79 episodes, 3692 segments, 12 speakers) with native-speaker-verified Japanese references, combining automatic intelligibility (Whisper re-transcription) and speaker-embedding similarity with a blind listening study by five JLPT-N1 raters. Among cloning systems, only GPT-SoVITS attains usable intelligibility (character error rate 0.215, against 1.152 for F5-TTS and 4.603 for CosyVoice2), while EdgeTTS is most intelligible overall (0.030). Critically, the automatic and perceptual measures dissociate: F5-TTS scores marginally higher on embedding similarity (0.729 vs. 0.722), yet raters preferr GPT-SoVITS three to one. Naturalness shows no detectable gap between GPT-SoVITS and EdgeTTS (mean opinion score 3.08 versus 3.12, p=0.93), a null result at a resolution of about 0.6 points. In a single-speaker probe, speaker similarity rises from 0.64 to 0.71 as the reference lengthens from 3 to 10 s. Embedding similarity alone is therefore an unreliable proxy for perceived speaker identity.

title: X-SLR: A Hexagonal Architecture Framework for Reporting Systematic Literature Reviews
abstract: Systematic literature reviews are essential for synthesizing scientific evidence but remain complex and resource-intensive processes that demand significant time and human effort. To reduce bias, they are usually conducted collaboratively and according to established methodologies. However, the way in which the process is documented, including the steps taken and the tools used, often depends on the author&rsquo;s preferences or basic guidelines of traditional methodologies. This variability makes it difficult to interpret the procedure and results and limits reproducibility for other researchers. This work introduces the Hexagonal Systematic Literature Review (X-SLR) architecture as a framework designed to standardize the reporting of procedures and results in systematic literature reviews. The X-SLR is based on the ports and adapters model from software engineering, which separates the core logic of a system from the tools and platforms used to implement it. Applied to reviews, the model conceptualizes the research goals as a central core connected to six functional components (ports): search strategy, selection criteria, data extraction, quality assessment, analysis and synthesis, and reporting. Each port can be linked to various tools through adapters. The proposed framework provides a structured mechanism for documenting review procedures, tool integration, and methodological decisions. By explicitly documenting port contracts, adapter choices, and traceability links, X-SLR is intended to help researchers assess whether tool substitutions preserve methodological coherence. A conceptual proposal, representative tool configurations, and a demonstration scenario are presented to illustrate the framework. The framework was retrospectively evaluated by applying a 25-item reporting checklist to a previously published SLR. Two independent coders achieved 88.0% agreement (Cohen&rsquo;s &kappa;=0.82), and the resulting Documentation Coverage score was 0.48. A separate internal formative assessment with two systematic review practitioners provided preliminary evidence regarding the clarity, traceability, complementarity, and usefulness of the X-SLR representation. These results provide preliminary evidence supporting X-SLR as a reporting and traceability artifact, while prospective studies are required to assess its effects on review execution, efficiency, and substantive reproducibility.

title: A Dated Corpus and a Seven-Layer Benchmark for Kazakhstani Legal Question Answering
abstract: Legal question answering is usually evaluated as if the law were static. In Kazakhstan, it changed twice within one year: a new Constitution replaced the 1995 text on 1 July 2026, and a new Tax Code replaced its predecessor on 1 January 2026, both reusing article numbers for different norms. We release a dated corpus of 41 Kazakhstani acts parsed to article level in both official languages (12,235 Russian and 11,973 Kazakh articles) and a benchmark of 150 question-answer pairs in seven layers, two of which score declining to answer and asking for a date. Two practising lawyers confirmed every pair. Comparing a no-retrieval baseline, retrieval-augmented generation and a tool-using agent, we find that retrieval rather than generation accounts for most citation error, measured against each pair&rsquo;s source articles: given the gold article, the model cites it in 92% of cases, and retrieval alone reduces citations of non-existent norms from 31% to zero. The agent adds nothing on this measure and abstains far less often. Dense retrieval improves citation recall but nearly doubles the repealed norms presented as current; date-aware ranking removes them for every retriever, although under dense retrieval it also removes three historically required citations. The retrieval findings are reproduced on two open models.

title: Structured Knowledge Extraction from Wheat Variety Approval Texts via Relation-Aware In-Context Learning and Progressive Knowledge Calibration
abstract: Knowledge extraction serves as a critical technique for constructing domain-specific knowledge graphs and enabling intelligent text parsing. In the vertical agricultural domain, wheat variety approval texts contain abundant agronomic trait entities and their relational associations. Nevertheless, they are characterized by dense domain-specific terminology, the co-occurrence of multiple relations, long entity spans, and mixed numerical and textual expressions, which pose considerable challenges to the accurate extraction of entity-relation triples. Existing in-context learning paradigms mostly retrieve demonstrations based on general-purpose semantic embeddings. The retrieved demonstrations rarely achieve relation-structure matching with query instances; furthermore, LLMs are susceptible to format hallucinations, which limit entity and relation extraction performance. Accordingly, we propose Relation-aware Demonstration Retrieval and Progressive Knowledge Calibration for In-Context Learning (ReCal-ICL), a relation-aware in-context learning framework for joint entity and relation extraction. ReCal-ICL employs RADS, a relation-aware demonstration selector based on hierarchical contrastive learning. Through hierarchical quadruples, in-batch dynamic negative sampling, and a hybrid loss, RADS reshapes the representation space to enhance relational-structure matching between retrieved demonstrations and query instances. In addition, a two-layer output constraint strategy is developed, which integrates prompt-template prior constraints and post hoc result verification mechanisms to jointly guarantee the format compliance of extraction outputs. We conduct comparative and ablation experiments on WVAD as well as public NYT and CoNLL04 datasets. Experimental results show that ReCal-ICL achieves competitive joint extraction performance across multiple datasets. Further experiments show that incorporating demonstrations benefits downstream extraction, while the retrieval relevance evaluation indicates that RADS improves the relational relevance of retrieved demonstrations.

title: A Textile Standardization Large Language Model Integrating LoRA Fine-Tuning and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Intelligent question answering for textile standards requires accurate domain understanding, clause retrieval, and evidence-grounded generation, yet general-purpose large language models often lack sufficient domain adaptation and factual support. This study proposes a textile-standard question-answering framework that integrates Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning with multidimensional retrieval-augmented generation (MDRAG). Based on 7017 domestic and international textile standards, we constructed a structured knowledge resource containing 121,166 annotated domain elements and a task-specific dataset of 2000 question&ndash;answer pairs. Qwen3.5-9B-Base, Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct, and GLM-4-9B were evaluated under three primary settings: Baseline, Baseline+LoRA, and Baseline+LoRA+MDRAG. A separate comparison with conventional RAG was conducted to assess the additional benefit of multidimensional retrieval over single-path retrieval. Among the primary settings, Qwen3.5-9B-Base with LoRA+MDRAG achieved the highest overall performance, with a cosine similarity of 0.624, a BLEU score of 0.283, and an expert-based overall score of 24.4. These findings support the use of lightweight domain adaptation together with multidimensional structured knowledge retrieval for textile-standard question answering.

title: Team Cognition Under Algorithmic Management: Evidence from Distributed Software Development Teams
abstract: Algorithmic systems increasingly shape how distributed software teams monitor work and evaluate performance, but their relationship with shared team understanding remains unclear. This study examined perceived algorithmic monitoring and evaluation (AME), supportive leadership, team mental models, and technical task-output performance in 72 distributed software development teams from 32 firms participating in Horizon Europe projects. Survey responses from 317 team members were averaged to team scores and matched with five GTmetrix indicators of each team&rsquo;s delivered output collected six months later. Averaged perceptions of AME and of supportive leadership were each positively associated with averaged perceived shared understanding. These associations held when the nesting of teams within firms was modeled, but between-team reliability of the aggregated measures was low (ICC(2) &le; 0.16), so they are associations among team-averaged perceptions rather than evidence of reliable differences in shared team cognition. AME showed nominal associations with two highly correlated technical indicators that did not survive adjustment for multiple testing and were weaker in a web-only subsample of 59 teams that excluded mobile applications measured through store listing pages; the indicators describe page performance under observed deployment conditions. No statistically detectable moderation by supportive leadership was found, and the exploratory, firm-unadjusted bootstrap gave no evidence of a conditional indirect association through team mental models. The study locates the empirical boundaries of a team-cognition account of algorithmic management: perceptual associations are present, but the proposed path to technical performance is not supported in these data.
