Cross-Modal Relation Preservation Knowledge Distillation from VLMs for Fine-Grained Visual Classification
abstract: <jats:p>Knowledge distillation has emerged as an effective approach to distill large-scale Vision-Language Models (VLMs) into lightweight networks under resource-constrained settings. However, existing VLM distillation methods typically transfer knowledge by matching output probabilities, requiring the student model to perform point-wise alignment with the teacher&apos;s predictive distribution, which may fail to fully exploit the rich relational information embedded in VLM visual-language similarities. To address this issue, we propose Cross-Modal Relational Preservation Knowledge Distillation(CMRP-KD), which directly integrates the multimodal knowledge of VLMs into a compact model during training and shifts the distillation objective from probability matching to relational structure preservation. Specifically, CMRP-KD models cross-modal relations from two complementary levels of the VLM visual-language similarity matrix, and employs Pearson correlation-based constraints to preserve the relative relational structure between the teacher and student, thereby enabling more effective transfer of cross-modal knowledge. Extensive experiments on multiple fine-grained image classification benchmarks demonstrate that CMRP-KD generally outperforms existing VLM distillation methods, improving classification accuracy while maintaining high inference efficiency without introducing any additional computational overhead during inference. The code is available at https://github.com/WMX1007/CMRP-KD.</jats:p>

How Evaluation Splits Reshape Conclusions in Short-Text Field Classification: A Case Study on Educational Data Domain Classification
abstract: <jats:p>Data classification and grading regulations require organizations to assign field-level semantic categories to structured data before sensitivity assessment, but short, context-poor field names make this nontrivial. We design and evaluate a character–word–sentence fusion architecture on a standardstraceable Chinese educational-field corpus (162 concepts drawn from seven Ministry-of-Education standards) under two evaluation protocols. Under aconventional sample-level split, character-only and word-only branches alone already approach ceiling performance (macro-F1 0.98 and 0.99), because the same concept’s naming variants recur across training and test and these fromscratch embeddings memorize surface patterns rather than learn transferable semantics. Under a concept-level held-out split, where no test-set concept’s name appears in training, the ranking reverses: over six partitions, characterand word-level branches degrade to mean macro-F1 0.38–0.39, while every combination including the pretrained sentence encoder scores substantially higher (0.51–0.56), a clean separation by whether the sentence branch is included. Enriching the input with the field’s textual explanation, intended to help weak-semantics fields, achieves a leaked perfect score under the samplelevel split but is consistently worse than the plain input under concept-level holdout, across all six partitions. A confirmatory case study on 142 real fields from a Chinese university reproduces the same leaked-perfect-score failure mode and shows that a real deployment can be too table-scarce to construct the recommended held-out check. These findings indicate that sample-level splits on field-classification corpora with repeated underlying concepts can substantially overstate generalization, and we argue that concept-level (or table-level) held-out evaluation should be reported alongside conventional splits for this task family.</jats:p>

title: Rafale: Towards the Efficient Resource-Aware Federated Knowledge Distillation on Heterogeneous Clients
abstract: <jats:p>Knowledge distillation is an highly effective machine learning technique for transferring knowledge from a large model, i.e., teacher, to a smaller model, i.e., student, improving model efficiency without sacrificing performance. This paper proposes a novel resource-aware federated learning framework Rafale that incorporates an adaptive client clustering mechanism based on computational resource availability and model complexity. High-resourceb clients train complex teacher models, and low-resource clients leverage distilled knowledge from teachers to train lightweight student models. Further, to optimize the aggregation process by introducing a clustering-based weightsharing mechanism that minimizes communication overhead while maintaining model accuracy. In this paper, a revolutionary Rafale framework that greatly reduces communication cost and separates model training from architectural constraints is proposed. To increase scalability and robustness, the suggested method makes use of resource-aware client selection, adaptive information sharing, and effective distillation techniques. In comparison to state-of-the-art FL approaches, experimental data show that RA-FKD delivers greater accuracy, decreases communication costs by up to 76%, and improves system efficiency. A cosine similarity loss KDC is introduced in knowledge distillation to improve the alignment between teacher and student models, enhancing knowledge transfer. Experimental evaluations on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets demonstrate that proposed framework achieving student test accuracy of 91.15% with reduction of 76.08% communication cost.</jats:p>

title: Knowledge Distillation and Explainability Analysis for Lightweight Retinal Disease Classification Using MultiEYE Fundus Images
abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: Class imbalance and probabilistic prediction quality are important considerations in lightweight retinal classification. We evaluated whether knowledge distillation (KD) from a ConvNeXtV2-Base teacher improved an EfficientNet-B0 student in nine-class MultiEYE fundus classification. Methods: Exact-content screening quarantined 131 of 58,036 records because of exact-content duplication or label conflicts. Six prespecified seeds were evaluated in no-KD, label-smoothing, and KD arms (18 runs) under matched training conditions. Within the controlled experiment, TEST data were not used for training, hyperparameter tuning, checkpoint or model selection, or protocol modification. The primary endpoint was the KD−no-KD macro-F1 difference on decontaminated TEST (n = 11,573), assessed by paired image-level bootstrap (10,000 replicates). Grad-CAM and Grad-CAM++ were examined qualitatively using one deterministically selected case per class and six-seed consensus maps. Results: Mean macro-F1 was 0.593, 0.597, and 0.633 for no-KD, label smoothing, and KD. KD exceeded no-KD by 0.039 (95% CI, 0.025–0.053; p < 0.001), with positive paired differences in all six seeds, and label smoothing by 0.036 (Holm-adjusted p < 0.001); label smoothing did not differ from no-KD (Holm-adjusted p = 0.554). Class-wise F1 differences were non-negative across all nine classes, with six remaining significant after correction for multiple comparisons. The Brier score difference was −0.077 (95% CI, −0.081 to −0.072; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001), while ECE decreased descriptively from 0.171 to 0.084. Nine-class Grad-CAM and direct Grad-CAM++ consensus maps enabled qualitative no-KD versus KD comparison without establishing lesion-localization superiority. Conclusions: KD improved macro-F1 and lowered the Brier score while retaining the same EfficientNet-B0 student at inference. The evaluated label-smoothing configuration did not reproduce the macro-F1 gain; clinical superiority and external generalizability remain unestablished.</jats:p>

Cross-Resolution Knowledge Distillation for Low-Compute Fine-Grained Bird Classification
abstract: <jats:p>Fine-grained visual classification relies on subtle local cues and is highly sensitive to input resolution, yet practical deployment often constrains image size and inference cost. Existing low-resolution recognition methods often depend on additional network structures or complex training modules, limiting deployment simplicity. This study evaluates a simple cross-resolution knowledge distillation (KD) strategy under a fixed low-compute constraint. The teacher receives higher-resolution inputs to provide richer class-discriminative visual knowledge, whereas the student is trained at 160×160 and is the only model retained for deployment. Both networks use ResNet-18, allowing resolution-aware supervision to be studied without changing the inference architecture. On the CUB-200-2011 dataset, the 160×160 baseline achieved 66.01±0.53% test accuracy. The 224→160 KD configuration improved accuracy to 70.15±0.63%, while the final 384→160 configuration with T = 4 , α = 0.75 , and a 30-epoch cosine schedule reached 71.60±0.68% accuracy and 71.56±0.62% macro-F1. The results also show that a stronger teacher does not automatically produce a stronger student: transfer quality depends on the balance between teacher supervision strength and student optimization. These findings support cross-resolution KD as a practical way to recover fine-grained information during training while preserving low-resolution inference cost.</jats:p>

Cross-DATA: Cross-Data Attention Distillation for Lightweight Sound Classification with Limited Data
abstract: <jats:p>Using the UrbanSound8K dataset as a representative case, this study investigates how lightweight acoustic models can be trained with limited labeled data in resource-constrained environments. Because conventional knowledge distillation confines knowledge transfer to a single target dataset, it leaves the rich prior knowledge in external audio sources largely unused. We therefore propose Cross-DATA, a framework that treats a large-scale, general audio dataset such as FSD50K as an auxiliary knowledge source and integrates a newly designed Cross-data Attention Distillation mechanism. With mixed data batches as input, a powerful teacher model establishes inter-feature correlation patterns that the compact student network is encouraged to reproduce. In this way, the teacher's generic acoustic representations and discriminative capabilities can be transferred beyond the distribution of the target data, rather than being reduced to data augmentation or feature imitation. Experiments on UrbanSound8K show that the resulting student model surpasses traditional single-dataset distillation approaches in classification accuracy while using only about 4% of the teacher model's parameters and computational cost. Cross-DATA consequently alleviates the representational capacity deficit of lightweight models in small-data scenarios.</jats:p>

BioScaleML: A Lakehouse-Based Framework for,Large-Scale Biomedical Text Classification
abstract: <jats:p>Objective: The exponential growth of unstructured biomedical text across scientific literature, clinical narratives, and registries requires scalable, privacy-conscious informatics infrastructure. Existing solutions often rely heavily on managed cloud ecosystems, creating data governance, cost, and vendor lock-in challenges. This study presents BioScaleML, an open-source, local Lakehouse architecture designed to integrate end-to-end biomedical data management, scalable distributed processing, and reproducible machine learning (ML) pipelines within a controlled on-premises environment.,Methods: BioScaleML was engineered by coupling Apache Spark for distributed computation, Delta Lake for ACID-compliant transactional storage and schema enforcement, Hadoop for local persistence, and a PostgreSQL-backed Hive metastore for unified metadata management. The framework was evaluated across two curated biomedical text corpora totaling 49,118 documents (19,681 PubMed-style abstracts and 29,437 full-text article sections) annotated across major oncological categories (breast, lung, and prostate). Standardized Extract-Transform-Load (ETL) pipelines engineered TF-IDF feature representations, feeding reusable ML pipelines trained on local hardware.,Results: The integrated architecture enabled deterministic dataset versioning, robust schema governance, and end-to-end workflow execution on commodity infrastructure without cloud reliance. Baseline classification models—including Multinomial Logistic Regression, Linear Support Vector Machines, and Multinomial Naive Bayes—achieved consistent high-throughput classification across both corpora (reaching up to 90.6% accuracy), demonstrating that enterprise-grade data management and NLP processing can be achieved locally.,Conclusion: BioScaleML provides a practical, cost-effective blueprint for healthcare and research institutions seeking reproducible biomedical text analytics under strict data sovereignty constraints. By establishing a transaction-aware foundation, BioScaleML provides an extensible framework for scaling local informatics pipelines to advanced domain-specific language models and multi-modal clinical datasets.</jats:p>

Forecasting Fine-Tuning Break-Even Label Budgets in Text Classification from Frozen Embedding Geometry
abstract: Choosing between zero-shot inference and supervised fine-tuning is often a label-budget decision: practitioners want to know when additional supervision will make adaptation worthwhile. Existing comparisons usually determine this threshold only after training models across multiple data budgets, leaving no low-cost way to anticipate it. We test whether class separability in frozen sentence-embedding spaces can serve as a training-free, although label-dependent, predictor of this break-even. Because separability itself requires class labels, the experiment deliberately evaluates a strong-form geometric signal rather than an annotation-free deployment rule. In a prospectively prespecified study spanning 35 public English-language text-classification tasks and three sentence encoders, we related pre-adaptation separability to the label budget at which a supervised Transformer classifier first exceeded a fixed instruction-tuned zero-shot comparator. Silhouette-based separability did not satisfy the prespecified inferential and practical-utility criteria, and an alternative separability measure produced a different directional pattern. Many tasks also failed to reach break-even within the tested budget, producing substantial right censoring. Censoring-aware, heteroskedasticity-robust, and influence-oriented post hoc analyses did not materially change the interpretation. Frozen embedding separability alone is therefore not a sufficiently stable estimator of fine-tuning break-even in this comparison regime. These findings place an empirical boundary on a plausible geometric heuristic and suggest that useful forecasts will likely require comparator-aware information, local boundary structure, or early adaptation dynamics.

Efficient numerical verification of probabilities and AUC in chemometric classification
abstract: <jats:p>Small probability errors can change the ordering of nearly tied chemometric predictions. I study the cost of certifying probabilities and the finite-set macro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for fixed encoded pairwise classifier outputs. A fast probability enclosure exploits classical M-matrix structure and falls back to inverse-defect verification or checked exact arithmetic. A complementary degree certificate allocates refinement when a nonzero AUC interval width is acceptable; the two workflows are evaluated separately. The application study includes 48 real-data tasks from six spectral datasets and retained gas-sensor and pathogen Raman outputs. Rational references covered 172926 probability coordinates without an enclosure failure. Ordinary calculation produced 33 strict ranking reversals and one spurious tie in two gas-sensor tasks, with maximum AUC error 0.000812. All 24 newly fitted spectral tasks already had correct ordinary AUC. On Rock and EthanolLevel, introduced after implementation optimization, certified postprocessing time decreased by 23.1% and 34.2% relative to inverse-defect verification at the same probability-width and exact-AUC requirements. Savings fell to 5.3% and 0.5% when preprocessing and classifier prediction were included. Separately, all 10368 calls in a 216-case budget study enclosed exact AUC and met their requested widths, but reduced refinement counts rarely translated into substantial time savings. These results support lower-cost numerical auditing on specified chemometric workloads, while delimiting its benefit relative to ordinary computation and predictive validation.</jats:p>

title: GLaDViT: interpretable gated fusion of frozen vision, text and layout features for document image classification
abstract: Classifying scanned pages by document type is a routing step in enterprisedocument processing. Layout-aware models reach high accuracy but rely onlarge-scale document pretraining and full fine-tuning, and seldom expose why adecision was made. We study a deliberately lightweight alternative, GLaDViT,which keeps CLIP and BERT encoders frozen, derives a layout descriptor fromTesseract hOCR word boxes, and trains only a gated fusion head. Because theclassifier is linear in the gated sum of modality embeddings, every class logitdecomposes exactly into per-modality terms, which yields an attribution that isfaithful to the computation by construction, unlike the gate weights alone. Ona label-corrected release of Tobacco-3482 (2737 pages, fixed 2186/272/279split), GLaDViT reaches \((93.7\pm0.4%)\) accuracy over three seeds (95% Wilsoninterval 90.2--96.0%), against 87.7% for the best single modality; addinglayout to vision and text contributes 2.8 accuracy points and gating a further1.1. The layout stream nevertheless receives at most about 10% of the gatemass, indicating that gate weights are mixing coefficients rather thanimportance scores. A triple InfoNCE alignment of the three streams, used as awarm-up on frozen features, lowers accuracy to 90.3%; we analyse this negativeresult. Code and hOCR tooling will be made publicly available.

Improved vision transformer for sports image classification via transfer learning and knowledge distillation
abstract: <jats:p>To address the challenges posed by complex visual characteristics in sports image classification, this study proposes an enhanced Vision Transformer (ViT) model built upon the Native Resolution ViT (NaViT) architecture. The principal innovations include replacing conventional single-layer feedforward networks with parallel feedforward networks and introducing an attention-guided distillation framework with input-dependent attention-weighted feature fusion, which adaptively regulates the contribution of frozen distillation features to the prediction pathway. The proposed approach leverages ImageNet-pretrained weights and performs domain-specific fine-tuning on sports datasets. Experimental results demonstrate substantial performance gains. On the multi-sport classification dataset, the proposed model achieves an accuracy of 0.9752 and a Macro-F1 score of 0.9753, outperforming the evaluated CNN benchmarks and ViT variants. For soccer match event classification, it achieves an accuracy of 0.9863 and a Macro-F1 score of 0.9718, while ranking first in the TOPSIS evaluation. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of integrating parallel feedforward processing, transfer learning, and distillation-guided feature fusion for sports image classification under complex visual conditions.</jats:p>

title: Multi-View Dual-Contrastive Graph Learning with Adaptive Agreement for Semi-Supervised Text Classification
abstract: Text classification with few labeled examples requires models that can effectively exploit unlabeled data while remaining lightweight. Graph-based approaches address this by modeling documents through their relations, but existing graph contrastive methods for text often rely on augmentations that alter semantic structure and are affected by unreliable false negatives. We propose Multi-View Dual-Contrastive Graph Learning (MDCGA), a framework that learns a shared document representation by integrating lexical, semantic, and keyword-based relational signals through enhanced dual contrastive objectives designed to reduce the impact of false negatives. Experiments on MR, Ohsumed, AG News, and R8 show that MDCGA achieves accuracies of 85.71%, 70.49%, 92.76%, and 97.40%, respectively. The approach demonstrates robustness in very low labeled settings, uses relatively few parameters, and shows limited sensitivity to hyperparameter choices.

title: Cost-Matrix-Assisted Evaluation of High-Performance Teacher-Guided Knowledge Distillation for Lightweight Aerial Disaster Classification
Unified Attention for Efficient Image Classification and Captioning
abstract: <jats:p>Transformers are the standard for visual representation learning and multimodal tasks like image captioning, but conventional multi-head attention relies on separate linear projections for queries, keys, and values, causing parameter redundancy and high computational cost. We propose Unified Attention, a parameter-efficient mechanism that reuses a single linear transformation across multiple attention passes. We instantiate this in Unified Vision Transformers (UViT) for image classification and Unified Transformers (UTR) for image captioning. Our approach reduces parameters per attention block by up to 75% while preserving essential structural dependencies and capturing consistent mappings between inputs and outputs. Experiments show that UTR improves image captioning metrics across multiple datasets, while UViT achieves competitive ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 83% with fewer parameters than baseline ViT. Unified Attention offers both a mapping-based interpretation of attention and a practical strategy for designing compact, efficient transformers for vision and multimodal tasks. The code for our experiments will be available on github upon acceptance.</jats:p>

Fidelity-Constrained Rule-Based Knowledge Distillation of Random Forests for Compact Breast Cancer Grade Classification
abstract: <jats:p>Breast cancer is a highly heterogeneous disease at the histopathological and molecular levels, and histological grade is a key prognostic indicator reflecting tumor biology. Although Random Forest models effectively capture nonlinear patterns in high-dimensional gene expression data, the decision logic of large tree ensembles remains difficult to inspect directly. This study proposes a knowledge-distillation framework that transfers the probabilistic decision behavior of a Random Forest teacher model to a compact, rule-based student model for distinguishing low- from high-histological-grade breast tumors using 20,385 gene-expression features from 1892 METABRIC samples, with clinical information used for sample matching and histological-grade label definition. Root-to-leaf decision paths extracted from the teacher were converted into a binary rule-activation matrix, followed by proximal group sparsification and fidelity-constrained Top-K rule selection. For the principal 400-tree teacher configuration, the student retained 65.0 ± 13.7 rules and achieved an ROC-AUC of 0.833 ± 0.023 and an average precision of 0.843 ± 0.019, while maintaining a raw teacher–student Pearson fidelity of 0.9607 ± 0.0112. As teacher capacity increased, the number of active decision paths increased substantially, whereas the selected rule budget remained within a comparatively narrow range and increased only modestly. The compact student also showed approximately 46% lower measured end-to-end inference latency and a 76% smaller serialized deployment size than the 400-tree teacher. Within the present METABRIC evaluation, these findings indicate that the structural complexity of a tree ensemble and the complexity required to approximate its probabilistic behavior need not scale proportionally, and that the proposed framework can provide a favorable trade-off among predictive performance, teacher fidelity, and deployment compactness.</jats:p>

title: Efficient Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting via Latency-Constrained Distillation and Dynamic Pruning
abstract: <jats:p>Multivariate time-series forecasting models often achieve improved prediction accuracy at the cost of increased model complexity and inference latency, limiting their deployment on resource-constrained computing platforms. In addition, lower parameter counts or theoretical computational costs do not necessarily lead to faster execution on actual hardware. To address this issue, we propose a Latency-Constrained Distillation and Dynamic Pruning (LCDP) framework for efficient multivariate time-series forecasting. LCDP introduces a latency-constrained adaptive optimization strategy that jointly considers forecasting loss, knowledge-distillation loss, local feature-alignment loss, and hardware inference latency during student-model training. Local feature-guided knowledge transfer is used to enhance the student model’s ability to capture fine-grained temporal patterns, while deployment-oriented dynamic structural pruning progressively adjusts the group-wise sparsity pattern of the student model according to latency feedback from the target hardware while retaining the original dense layer dimensions. Experiments on the ETTh1, ETTm1, and ETTm2 datasets using two CPU platforms show that LCDP achieves competitive forecasting accuracy with a lightweight student inference backbone containing 7336 active parameters and requiring 50,848 dense multiply-accumulate operations. The saved student checkpoint additionally contains 2080 parameters in a training-time feature-alignment projection that is not invoked during inference. LCDP provides an effective balance between forecasting accuracy and practical inference efficiency, demonstrating its potential for low-latency multivariate time-series forecasting on CPU-based resource-constrained platforms.</jats:p>

title: SAS Multimetric Tribunal: Structural Classification of Hallucination in AI-Generated Text – What a Benchmark Design Can and Cannot Show
abstract:
<jats:p>Hallucination-detection systems are usually judged by a single headline metric, computed under a benchmark design that determines what that metric can show. This paper’s contribution is not a detection algorithm — structural coherence scoring is established — but a methodology for measuring exactly what a benchmark proves and what it does not, applied to the SAS Multimetric Tribunal: a seven-module, GPU-free structural classifier combining lexical, entity-mutation, curvature, and logical-inversion signals via a cascading multiplicative penalty (\(\kappa_{D} = 0.56\), \(\kappa_{R} = 0.15\)).

On a stratified 1,800-pair benchmark (HaluEval-Dialogue, HaluEval-QA, TruthfulQA), the tribunal reaches F1 = 98.99% with zero false positives under an A\(\rightarrow\)A identical-text sanity check — matched or exceeded by trivial baselines, including exact string matching (F1 = 100%). We report this explicitly: a benchmark that cannot fail on identical text cannot establish precision. Under a real negative control (R3: 127 valid paraphrase pairs), every method tested fails — the tribunal flags 126/127 as hallucinations (specificity 0.8%), matched by simple lexical baselines. No lexical-overlap method in our comparison distinguishes a valid paraphrase from a hallucination.

We also report, as direct ablations rather than argument, that multiplicative combination outperforms weighted averaging of the same seven modules by 87.97 F1 points, and that SourceTargetGuard’s measured contribution is 3 of 1,800 true positives (0.17% of recall). The tribunal’s contribution is not a solved precision problem: it is an auditable, per-module architecture on which a semantic-equivalence guard can be added and measured — something a single-metric baseline offers no place to attach. This revision also reports a forensic audit distinguishing an earlier version’s undocumented-but-reproducible metrics from a stale sub-count, corrected in response to independent peer review.</jats:p>

title: Sequential Shared-LoRA Adaptation of BERT for Text Classification: A Continual-Learning Baseline
abstract: <jats:p>Fine-tuning a pre-trained language model separately for every classification task is costly in computation and storage, and scales poorly when tasks arrive over time. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) reduces this cost, but whether a single shared adapter can serve several classification tasks trained one after another remains underexplored. We study a frozen BERT-base backbone with one shared LoRA adapter in its self-attention layers and lightweight task-specific heads, trained sequentially on three tasks derived from the aclImdb movie-review corpus: binary sentiment, a rating-bucket task derived from the 1–10 review ratings, and a heuristic five-class genre task built from keyword rules, since the corpus has no genre metadata. The adapter and heads together comprise 302,602 of 109,784,842 parameters (0.2756%), cutting estimated storage for three tasks by 66.5% relative to per-task full fine-tuning. Each task peaks immediately after its own training stage (sentiment 88.6%, rating 89.1% against a 50% majority baseline, genre 57.2%). Sequential training, however, causes measurable forgetting: sentiment accuracy falls monotonically to 81.7% (forgetting score 0.0697) and rating accuracy from 89.1% to 83.5% (0.0550). These single-run results show that a compact shared adapter can support several related tasks while exposing interference under sequential adaptation, and they provide a reference accuracy–retention trade-off against which architecture-, regularization- and replay-based continual-learning mitigations can be evaluated.</jats:p>

title: SmolVLA-Diff: efficient knowledge distillation for VLA models for vertical task deployment
abstract: <jats:p>This paper systematically compared the high performance π0 model with the high efficiency SmolVLA model. Real machine evaluation revealed that π<sub>0</sub> relying on its powerful flow matching action of generator and huge VLM model number, precision lead in vertical task; While SmolVLA through lightweight attention head and asynchronous reasoning stack, on delay, power consumption and anti-jamming advantage is obvious. In order to integrate the advantages of the two models, we innovatively propose an action knowledge distillation method at the output layer to transfer the action strategy knowledge of the π<sub>0</sub> model to SmolVLA, so that it can obtain similar performance improvement to the former with negligible additional overhead. This study provides an effective performance enhancement scheme for the efficient and practical deployment of the robot VLA model.</jats:p>

title: Dual-Space Knowledge Distillation with Cross-Geometric Feature Interaction for Hyperspectral Image Classification
abstract: <jats:p>Hyperspectral image (HSI) classification is critical for remote sensing but faces challenges in balancing accuracy and inference efficiency. Existing graph-based knowledge distillation (KD) methods are confined to single geometric spaces, ignoring the hierarchical semantics of land-cover categories. Cross-geometry distillation compresses multiple geometries into a single Euclidean student, forcing one geometry to collapse into the other. In this paper, we propose Dual-Space Knowledge Distillation (DSKD), a novel dual-student dual-space KD framework integrating Euclidean (GCN) and Hyperbolic (HGCN) teachers to jointly train a native MLP student and a native HNN student. With cross-geometric feature bridging (CGFB) and output distribution cohesion (ODC), the two students mutually learn each other’s complementary geometry, so DSKD captures complementary spatial-spectral and hierarchical features while enabling graph-free inference without message passing. Extensive experiments on four HSI datasets and four general graph benchmarks demonstrate that DSKD outperforms single-space distillation and single-student cross-geometry baselines in most settings, confirming its effectiveness and generalization capability across diverse graph-structured data.</jats:p>

title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Medical Named Entity Recognition: An Empirical Study of LoRa on Biomedical Text
Multi-Level Contrastive Knowledge Distillation for Resource-efficient Visual Inference on Edge Devices
Dual-Domain Calibration with Source Rehearsal and Knowledge Distillation for Robust Cross-Dataset Classification
abstract: <jats:p>Automated peripheral blood cell classification has shown strong performance on curated microscopic image datasets, but model reliability can decrease when images are acquired from external sources with different visual characteristics. This study presents a reproducible deep learning protocol for five-class peripheral blood cell morphology classification involving basophils, eosinophils, lymphocytes, monocytes and neutrophils. The protocol compared five pretrained architectures, including Swin-Tiny, ConvNeXt-Tiny, MaxViT-Tiny, DeiT-Small and EfficientNetV2-B0, using balanced PBC training, validation and locked-test splits, followed by external zero-shot testing, image-quality stress evaluation and external-domain calibration. Initial PBC-only training produced high internal test performance but substantially lower external zero-shot performance, indicating a dataset-shift problem. To address this, we developed a source-retaining dual-domain calibration strategy that combines external calibration data, PBC rehearsal samples and teacher distillation. DeiT-Small was selected as the calibration backbone because it provided the strongest balance between PBC performance, stress robustness and external zero-shot generalisation. On locked testing, the proposed approach achieved a macro-F1 score of 0.9933 on the PBC test set and 0.9746 on the external test set. External class-wise performance remained high across all five cell categories, with macro precision, recall and F1 of approximately 0.9747, 0.9747 and 0.9746, respectively. These findings suggest that source-retaining calibration can improve cross-dataset generalisation while preserving source-domain performance. The study provides a transparent evaluation framework for assessing robustness, external validity and domain-shift effects in microscopic blood-cell image classification.</jats:p>

title: Toward scalable generative AI: efficient language model distillation via zero-shot rationales
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This paper investigates an efficient approach for distilling Large Language Models (LLMs) into smaller, application-specific models using zero-shot Chain of Thought (CoT) rationale generation and Optimization by Prompting (OPRO). To address the challenges of deploying computationally intensive generative AI for narrow tasks or resource-constrained environments, the approach leverages LLM reasoning capabilities to generate both labels and natural language explanations for unlabeled data. By reducing reliance on human-generated annotations, the approach substantially lowers annotation requirements and prompting costs while maintaining comparable performance in the evaluated settings. We formulate distillation as a multi-task learning problem in which student models are trained to jointly predict labels and learn from teacher-generated rationales, with the goal of improving data efficiency and generalization. Building on established zero-shot Chain of Thought (CoT) prompting and the OPRO prompt optimization technique, we use teacher-generated rationales to reduce annotation token requirements and examine the associated performance and efficiency gains. Additionally, we systematically investigate how explanation properties affect distillation efficiency. Across natural language inference and question answering benchmarks, results indicate that near-optimal performance can be achieved even when rationales are provided for only a subset of the training data, and that shorter explanations are often sufficient. These findings provide practical insights into the trade-offs between rationale generation cost and student model performance. Overall, this work contributes empirical evidence on the effectiveness and cost characteristics of rationale-based distillation for training compact, task-specific language models with minimal human intervention.</jats:p>

title: A multi-scale semantic perception network with multi-relational text graphs for text classification
Content in Graph Clothing: Structural Link Prediction Does Not Beat a Text Baseline for Weakness Classification of Vulnerability Reports
abstract: <jats:p>A vulnerability report is a short text, a CVE description, and a common task is to assign it a weakness class, a CWE. One appealing way to do this is to build a graph, connect each report to the terms of its description and each weakness to the terms of its known reports, and predict a report-to-weakness link with a structural index such as Adamic-Adar that scores a candidate by its shared neighbours. We ask whether this graph machinery earns its keep, by measuring it against the plainest alternative, ranking weaknesses by the cosine similarity of the report text to known reports. On 560 real vulnerability reports across 7 weakness classes from the National Vulnerability Database, with five-fold cross-validation and held-out report-to-weakness links, the content baseline recovers the correct weakness with a recall at one of 0.838 and a mean reciprocal rank of 0.898, and every structural index is worse, common neighbours at 0.764, Jaccard at 0.761, and Adamic-Adar lowest at 0.616. Adding the structural score to the content baseline does not help, the ensemble reaches 0.832 against the baseline's 0.838, so the graph carries no signal the text does not, and a stronger supervised text classifier over the same features widens the gap to 0.921, so the structural indices lose to any reasonable text method. The reason is specific and mechanical. Because the graph is built from the report text, a structural link is a term-overlap score in disguise, and Adamic-Adar's rule of weighting a shared neighbour by the inverse log of its degree up-weights rare, off-topic terms and down-weights the diagnostic terms, sql, traversal, scripting, which occur in a moderate fraction of reports, a median of 15 percent, so its weighting is misaligned with the task. The conclusion is that when a graph is derived from content, structural link prediction is content similarity in graph clothing, and a worse-weighted one, so it should be measured against a text baseline before it is adopted. We release the corpus split and the harness.</jats:p>

AKDF: Adaptive knowledge distillation for secure, efficient, copyright-protected model publishing
abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The rise of large language models (LLMs) has transformed natural language processing, powering applications from creative writing to code generation. However, their vast size and proprietary nature present two major challenges, including efficient deployment on limited hardware and secure protection of intellectual property. This work introduces the Adaptive Knowledge Distillation Framework (AKDF), a unified training approach that simultaneously com-presses LLMs and embeds ownership signals for copyright assurance. AKDF employs parameter-efficient Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to distill a 1-billion-parameter student model from an 8-billion-parameter teacher while integrating an output-level watermarking module directly into the distillation process. This design reduces trainable parameters and encodes verifiable ownership signatures without altering the frozen base weights. Experiments on ARC-Easy, PIQA, and WMT16 show that the student retains approximately 76% of the teacher’s performance while maintaining competitive reasoning and translation quality under substantial compression. AKDF also enables secure and communication-efficient model publishing, providing a practical path to-ward bandwidth-efficient and ownership-aware deployment of large-scale language models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Dual-Teacher Personalized Federated Learning with Hyper-Knowledge Distillation for Breast Ultrasound Classification
Preference-Emergence Anchor Distillation for Efficient Generative Reward Modeling
Universal Noise Augmentation (UNA): A Unified Training-Time Framework for Robust Multilingual Text Classification
abstract: <jats:p>Reliable multilingual text classification systems must tolerate surface-level noise without losing clean-input performance. Existing robustness toolkits provide perturbation libraries and evaluation workflows, but they do not by themselves define a compact training-time protocol that jointly controls perturbation scope, severity, sampling, and clean-noisy exposure. We introduce Universal Noise Augmentation (UNA), a unified training-time framework that integrates character-, token-, and structural-level perturbations with configurable intensity, clean-noisy mixing, operator sampling, and epoch-aware dynamic resampling. UNA is a protocol-level contribution rather than a claim of new primitive corruption operators, and it requires no modification to the classifier architecture or loss. We evaluate UNA with XLM-RoBERTa-base in three multilingual classification settings: cross-lingual natural language inference (MultiNLI→XNLI), intent classification (MASSIVE), and sentiment classification (Amazon Reviews Multilingual). Evaluation separates clean data, an in-family synthetic-noise stress test, and fixed task-specific noisy subsets, and includes ablations of intensity, clean-noisy ratio, sampling strategy, and dynamic versus static augmentation. Across six noisy task-tier comparisons, UNA improves accuracy by 6.8–8.5 percentage points, while clean accuracy changes by at most 0.4 percentage points. The results support UNA as a practical, architecture-preserving robustness-training configuration for engineering multilingual classification pipelines under the evaluated conditions.</jats:p>

title: Anti-Forgetting Adaptive Teacher-Driven Knowledge Distillation for Medical Image Classification
abstract: <jats:p>Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success in medical image classification, yet their performance remains sensitive to dataset size. Knowledge distillation (KD) alleviates this issue by transferring knowledge from a high-capacity teacher to a lightweight student. However, conventional KD relies on a static teacher, while adaptive teacher updating may improve performance on the student-learning data while reducing retention of knowledge acquired during teacher pretraining. To address these limitations, we propose an Anti-forgetting Adaptive Teacher-driven Knowledge Distillation framework (A2T-KD), which aims to balance teacher adaptation and pretraining-knowledge retention. The proposed framework integrates three modules: MITR for cross-epoch representation consistency, DSDO for prediction-space decoupling and class discriminability, and SGKD for feature- and logit-level knowledge transfer. Across nine medical imaging datasets, A2T-KD achieved higher mean values than the fixed-teacher Vanilla KD baseline in 30 of 36 dataset–metric comparisons. It also exhibited the lowest pretraining-set ACC degradation among the evaluated teacher-update baselines on all nine datasets, supporting the intended balance between teacher adaptation and pretraining-knowledge retention under the evaluated settings.</jats:p>

title: Autonomous Coding Agents for Software Development Testing and Debugging
abstract: <jats:p>Autonomous coding agents build on top of large language models to provide more action according to code suggestions: auto code officers look at files, code suggestions, edit, run tools, create tests, debug failures, and iterate over patches. This paper presents an overview of the existing knowledge regarding their application in the development, testing and debugging of software and suggests a guided lifecycle towards their application in production. The analysis differentiates between model capability and system capability in that the ability to retrieve a repository, interfaces of tools, execution environment, a test oracle, memory and approval gates are what would determine whether an agent could come up with a reliable change. Benchmarks have demonstrated high improvement in the initial results of SWE-bench to more interactive and structured repair systems, but the benchmark contamination, weak tests, underspecified problems, cost variance and non-equivalent evaluation environments provide hindrance to the straightforward leaderboard comparisons. It suggests a five-step operating model which includes, specifying the task, localizing the repository, implementation of the task by constrained means, validation through evidence and integration control. The architecture integrates sandboxed, least-privilege credentials, provenance capturing, policy-as-code, independent test generation, human inspection and rollback. Benchmark evidence, lifecycle coverage and autonomy risk tradeoffs, and validation controls are grouped into four figures of analysis and four tables. The research concludes that coding agents prove to be most useful with as a supervised engineering system and not as an unconditioned substitute of the developers. Measuring functional correctness, regression risk, security, maintainability, cost and operational safety is a combination needed to be taken to ensure that adoption is reliable. The research does not claim an original experiment on human subjects or production and explicit figures of the models are mentioned.</jats:p>

title: Debug2Fix: Can Interactive Debugging Help Coding Agents Fix More Bugs?
In the Age of AI Coding Agents, Keeping the Engineer in Software Engineering (Keynote)
AutoCodeSherpa: Symbolic Explanations in AI Coding Agents
abstract: <jats:p>Large language model (LLM) agents integrate external tools with one or more LLMs to accomplish specific tasks. Agents have rapidly been adopted by developers, and they are starting to be deployed in industrial workflows, such as their use to fix static analysis issues from the widely used SonarQube static analyzer. However, the growing importance of agents means their actions carry greater impact and potential risk. Thus, to use them at scale, an additional layer of trust and evidence is necessary. This work presents AutoCodeSherpa, a technique that provides explanations of software issues in the form of symbolic formulae. Inspired by the reachability, infection, and propagation model of software faults, the explanations are composed of input, infection, and output conditions, collectively providing a specification of the issue. In practice, the symbolic explanation is implemented as a combination of a property-based test (PBT) and program-internal symbolic expressions. Critically, this means our symbolic explanations are executable and can be automatically evaluated, unlike natural language explanations. Experiments show the generated conditions are highly accurate. For example, input conditions from AutoCodeSherpa had an accuracy of 85.7%. This high accuracy makes symbolic explanations particularly useful in two scenarios. First, the explanations can be used in automated issue resolution environments to decide whether to accept or reject patches from issue resolution agents; AutoCodeSherpa could reject 2x as many incorrect patches as baselines did. Second, as agentic AI approaches continue to develop, program analysis driven explanations like ours can be provided to other LLM-based repair techniques which do not employ analysis to improve their output. In our experiments, our symbolic explanations could improve the plausible patch generation rate of the Agentless technique by 60%.</jats:p>

Agentic Refactoring: An Empirical Study of AI Coding Agents
abstract:
<jats:p>Agentic coding tools, such as OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, and Cursor, are changing how software is developed. These AI-powered systems function as autonomous teammates capable of planning and executing complex development tasks. Agents have become active participants in refactoring, a key practice for improving internal code quality without altering observable behavior. Despite their increasing adoption, there is little empirical understanding of how agentic refactoring is used in practice, how it compares to human-driven refactoring, and what impact it has on code quality.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>To address this empirical gap, we present a large-scale study of AI agent-generated refactorings in real-world open-source Java projects, analyzing 51,412 refactoring instances across 12,256 pull requests and 14,998 commits based on the AIDev dataset. Our empirical analysis shows that refactoring is a common and intentional activity in this development paradigm, with agents explicitly targeting refactoring in 26.1% of commits. The subsequent analyses of refactoring types, purposes, and code quality focus on the 3,907 commits (32,611 instances) with explicit refactoring intent. Analysis of refactoring types reveals that high-level refactorings form the largest category overall. However, agentic refactoring contains a slightly larger share of lowlevel, consistency-oriented edits than human refactoring (27.6% vs. 24.4%), and its two most frequent operations are Rename Variable (7.6%) and Change Variable Type (6.8%). Additionally, the stated motivations behind agentic refactoring focus overwhelmingly on internal quality concerns (with 52.5% in maintainability and 28.1% in readability), although the measured metric improvements from these frequently occurring low-level refactorings remain limited. Furthermore, quantitative evaluation of code quality metrics shows that agentic refactoring yields small but statistically significant improvements in structural metrics, particularly for medium-level changes, reducing class size and complexity.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence Coding Agents in Software Engineering Education:: Why Development & Operations and Scale Matter
Same Task, Different Fate: Population Structure in Trajectory-Based Analyses of Coding Agents
Vibe Coding: An experiment with test-driven development
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Context</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Conversational Large Language Models (CLLMs) can automatically generate code by collaborating with users through natural language. However, poor collaboration can lead to poor quality output.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This exploratory study aims to investigate how humans and CLLMs can collaborate as peers through vibe coding, an approach that integrates principles from prompt engineering, agile design, and human-AI co-creation to enhance collaboration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We designed four interaction models representing different collaboration patterns in the software development process: the solo model (human-only development), the collaborative model (human–CLLM collaboration), the fully automated model (development autonomously performed by a CLLM), and the agentic model (development autonomously performed by the MetaGPT X platform). Based on these models, we implemented corresponding Test-Driven Development (TDD) workflows using structured prompts and Python scripts. We then conducted a controlled pre-experimental study with TDD professionals to compare the solo and collaborative workflows. In addition, we performed repeated exploratory executions of fully automated and agentic workflows on the same development tasks to obtain complementary evidence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our findings suggest that the choice of interaction model should depend on the development objective. Agentic workflows are best suited for rapid development and functionally correct production code but may introduce additional implementation complexity. However, they may also introduce additional implementation decisions that are not explicitly required by the functional specifications, resulting in untested decision points. In contrast, collaborative workflows produce higher-quality, better-organized test suites.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our work explored how humans can collaborate with CLLMs in generating code in highly intensive and demanding development process. Our results also show that accurately reproducing development process workflows is yet an open problem, also in the new agentic technologies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

Characterizing the Adoption of Autonomous Coding Agents in Functional Programming Repositories
abstract: <jats:p>Autonomous coding agents are increasingly participating in collaborative software development, yet little is known about their adoption in functional programming ecosystems. This paper presents an empirical study on the adoption of autonomous coding agents in GitHub repositories developed with functional programming languages. We analyzed 35 repositories written in Elixir, Haskell, F#, Erlang and OCaml, comprising 158 AI-generated Pull Requests. The results show that AI-generated contributions are already present in mature and actively maintained functional programming repositories. Most Pull Requests are small and incremental. OpenAI Codex accounts for 78 of the 93 AI-generated Pull Requests in Elixir repositories, whereas GitHub Copilot is responsible for 38 of the 39 Pull Requests identified in F# repositories. Elixir also presents the highest Pull Request acceptance rate (77.4%), while repository popularity exhibits no meaningful association with AI-generated Pull Request activity (𝜌 = −0.029 for stars and 𝜌 = −0.038 for forks).</jats:p>

AI-Assisted Software Engineering: Evaluating Copilot, Cursor, and Autonomous AI Agents for Rapid Application Development
abstract: <jats:p>The integration of large language models into software development tooling has produced a spectrum of assistance paradigms, from inline code completion to autonomous multi-step agents capable of navigating repositories and executing commands. This paper presents an empirical evaluation of three representative systems GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and autonomous agentic IDEs across a rapid application development task set. We assess effectiveness (does the generated application satisfy stated requirements?), efficiency (time to completion relative to unaided baselines), iteration behavior (error detection and corrective actions), and code quality outcomes (vulnerability rates, technical debt indicators). Our synthesis of controlled trials, enterprise telemetry studies, and standardized benchmarks finds a consistent pattern: AI assistance substantially accelerates low-complexity, high-boilerplate development tasks, but performance degrades sharply as task horizon and cross-file coherence requirements increase. Autonomous agents complete only a small fraction of end-to-end feature development tasks that short-horizon benchmarks suggest they can handle. Security vulnerability rates in generated code remain high across tools. We conclude with a practical framework for selecting assistance paradigms by task characteristics, and with an assessment of the gap between marketed capability and demonstrated capability.</jats:p>

title: An Empirical Investigation of Multi-Trial Consistency, Trajectory Pathologies, and Reliability Rankings in Software Engineering Agents
abstract: Autonomous software engineering (SWE) agents powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved notable milestones on repository-scale benchmarks such as SWE-bench. However, prevailing evaluation methodologies rely almost exclusively on single-trial resolution rates (pass@1). In real-world software maintenance and continuous integration (CI/CD) pipelines, single-trial success is an inadequate proxy for software reliability; an agent that succeeds on one invocation but fails on subsequent identical runs introduces non-deterministic flakiness and high human verification overhead. This paper contributes: (1) a prospective evaluation protocol designed to measure multi-trial consistency and trajectory pathologies across a 7,200-episode factorial grid (120 tasks × 6 models × 2 scaffolds × 5 trials), (2) formal metric formulations for empirical per-attempt pass rates ($\hat{p}_{attempt}$), strict all-trial consistency (AllPass@k), completion rates ($CR, JCR_k$), and Patch Churn Ratio (PCR), and (3) an operational feasibility pilot across 312 completed episodes on Google Gemini Flash models using SWE-agent (ACI) and OpenHands (CodeAct). The pilot demonstrates the operational feasibility of trajectory-level telemetry collection and reveals a 13.3% infrastructure censoring rate (8.9% provider API timeouts, 4.4% container resets), establishing the measurement foundations required for subsequent full-scale empirical reliability benchmarking.

title: Causally Sound Memory Invalidation For Long-Horizon Software Engineering Agents: Transitive Constraints, Partial Observability, And Verification Budgets
abstract: <jats:p>Long-horizon coding agents depend on compressed or persistent memories of past tool outputs, repository observations, design constraints, and derived engineering decisions. When a repository changes, a remembered observation may remain historically true while no longer justifying an active decision. Existing retrieval, compression, and state-consistent memory systems address portions of this challenge, but reliable selective transitive invalidation under missing dependencies and bounded verification resources remains a sharply defined research target. We formulate engineering memory as a time-indexed, provenance-annotated justification hypergraph; distinguish observation validity, justification validity, and current action admissibility; and propose CAVI (Causal Assumption Verification and Invalidation), a research architecture combining change-impact analysis, dependency closure, uncertainty-aware verification, and guarded handoff. We specify conditional soundness guarantees for complete dependency graphs, illustrate unavoidable limits when dependencies are latent, and outline a reproducible benchmark with counterfactual repository mutations. The contribution here is a formal and experimental research agenda, not empirical evidence that CAVI outperforms prior systems.</jats:p>

title: Perbandingan Kinerja Model Machine Learning dalam Memprediksi Konsumsi Bahan Bakar Kendaraan
abstract: <jats:p>Penelitian ini membahas upaya prediksi konsumsi bahan bakar kendaraan berbasis algoritma machine learning untuk mendukung efisiensi energi dan pengurangan emisi karbon. Sektor transportasi merupakan kontributor signifikan terhadap konsumsi energi nasional, sehingga diperlukan model prediksi akurat yang dapat digunakan dalam perencanaan kebijakan. Penelitian ini bertujuan membandingkan kinerja tiga algoritma regresi Decision Tree (DT), Random Forest (RF), dan Support Vector Machine (SVM) dalam memprediksi konsumsi bahan bakar berdasarkan fitur teknis kendaraan. Dataset yang digunakan bersumber dari Natural Resources Canada, terdiri dari variabel seperti kapasitas mesin, silinder, transmisi, emisi CO₂, dan konsumsi bahan bakar. Proses pra-pemrosesan mencakup one-hot encoding, normalisasi, dan pembagian data (hold-out 80:20). Evaluasi dilakukan menggunakan metrik RMSE, MAE, dan koefisien determinasi (R²). Hasil menunjukkan bahwa model Decision Tree memiliki performa terbaik dengan nilai RMSE terendah (0.326), MAE terendah (0.22), dan R² tertinggi (0.960), mengungguli Random Forest dan SVR. Temuan ini menunjukkan bahwa model sederhana namun tepat guna dapat lebih unggul dari model kompleks dalam kondisi dataset tertentu. Penelitian ini memberikan kontribusi terhadap pengembangan sistem prediktif efisiensi energi kendaraan dan dapat digunakan sebagai dasar untuk kebijakan transportasi berkelanjutan</jats:p>

title: BDD-Bench: A Behavior-Driven Benchmark for Coding Agents across the Application Lifecycle
AttnCompress: Dynamic Attention-Guided Trajectory Compression for Software Engineering Agents
abstract: <jats:p>The transition from human-centric assistance to Autonomous Software Engineering (ASE) agents has enabled the resolution of complex real-world SE tasks. However, the trial-and-error nature of these agents generates lengthy interaction trajectories, creating severe bottlenecks in terms of context window limits and cost. While context compression offers a potential remedy, prior approaches suffer from static pruning strategies and granularity mismatches, often failing to preserve the semantic dependencies and syntactic details crucial for SE tasks. To strictly preserve critical task evidence while reducing context length, we introduce AttnCompress, a dynamic attention-guided trajectory compression framework. Unlike existing approaches, AttnCompress bridges the gap between semantic integrity and dynamic adaptability through three key mechanisms: (1) structure-aware segmentation via perplexity (PPL) spikes to preserve the syntactic structure of code and logs; (2) relevance estimation using proxy attention weights to quantify the precise relevance of historical blocks to the agent’s current reasoning; and (3) a dynamic rolling window to re-evaluate and recall historical context as the task evolves. Extensive evaluation on SWE-Bench-Verified and Multi-SWE-Bench demonstrates that AttnCompress achieves a pass rate of 53.17%, outperforming prior state-of-the-art baselines while reducing token consumption by 21.6% and total costs by 33.6%. The framework proves to be model-agnostic and generalizes effectively across diverse programming languages.</jats:p>

title: Test-Oriented Programming: rethinking coding for the GenAI era
Red-Teaming Coding Agents from a Tool-Invocation Perspective: An Empirical Security Assessment
abstract:
<jats:p>Coding agents powered by large language models are becoming central modules of modern IDEs. They help users to perform various complex coding tasks by invoking tools. Although powerful, tool-invocation operation in coding agents opens a substantial attack surface for adversaries. Prior work has demonstrated attacks against both general-purpose LLM agents and domain-specific agents. However, to our knowledge, no previous works focus on the security risks of tool-invocation in coding agents. To fill this gap, we conduct the first systematic, in-depth red-teaming from a tool-invocation perspective in six popular real-world coding agents: Cursor, Claude Code, Copilot, Windsurf, Cline, and Trae.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Our red-teaming proceeds in two phases. In Phase 1, we conduct a prompt leakage as reconnaissance to recover system prompts and related context. Specifically, we identify a mode gap between chat generation and tool-call argument generation: during schema-driven argument completion, the model behaves as if it is performing benign structured filling and may copy hidden agent context into tool-call arguments. We instantiate this gap as ToolLeak, which exfiltrates agent-internal prompts (e.g., system prompts and tool metadata) via required tool parameters. In Phase 2, we hijack the tool-invocation behavior of the coding agent with a novel two-channel prompt injection in the tool description and the tool return. Our hijacking achieves remote code execution (RCE) on major real-world coding agents. We adaptively construct the malicious payload using leaked security information in Phase 1.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Our evaluation shows that ToolLeak substantially outperforms strong prompt-leak baselines in both emulated and real-world settings. In the emulated setting, ToolLeak achieves the best overall prompt-exfiltration performance across all six simulated coding agents. On real-world coding agents, ToolLeak achieves the best pseudo-recall on 18 of 25 evaluated agent-LLM pairs. Furthermore, our red-teaming successfully hijacks all six real-world coding agents for RCE and consistently yields higher attack success rates than baseline attacks. Lastly, we present two case studies on Cursor and Claude Code to demonstrate the real-world impact of our red-teaming.</jats:p>

SEBGen: A Self-Evolving Benchmark Generation Framework for Software Engineering Agents
abstract: <jats:p>Static software engineering benchmarks such as SWE-bench suffer from three fundamental limitations: task sets are fixed and become saturated as model capabilities rapidly improve; expert construction is costly and slow; and difficulty levels cannot adapt to evolving model abilities. We present SEBGen, a self-evolving benchmark generation framework that synthesizes evaluation tasks from code repositories and improves its generation strategies through an evolution loop. SEBGen introduces three key innovations: an explicit five-dimension exploration value evaluator that quantitatively scores generation strategies across quality, novelty, difficulty coverage, skill diversity, and evolution potential, replacing implicit LLM judgments; a five-layer hybrid validation pipeline combining mechanical checks with LLM-as-judge evaluation; and a self-evolving loop with archive-based experience accumulation, sigmoid-scaled parent selection, and LLM-driven strategy mutation. On a synthetic corpus, SEBGen achieves a 96 percent validation pass rate with stable quality across five evolution generations. On a real repository, it transforms all six tqdm bug-fix commits into validated tasks, and a comparison against SWE-bench Lite shows task quality of 0.76 approaching expert baselines of 0.80. These results indicate that dynamic, self-evolving benchmarks are a viable alternative to static benchmarks.</jats:p>

RAILFUN: Aplikasi Multimedia On Demand Berbasis Chat Bot Sebagai Layanan Hiburan Pada Kereta API
abstract: <jats:p>Perjalanan kereta api yang panjang sering kali menimbulkan kebosanan bagi penumpang, terutama dengan minimnya fitur hiburan mandiri dan keterbatasan akses internet. Penelitian ini mengusulkan pengembangan aplikasi "Railfun: Aplikasi Multimedia On Demand Berbasis Chatbot Sebagai Layanan Hiburan Pada Kereta Api" untuk mengatasi permasalahan tersebut. Tujuan utama penelitian ini adalah mengembangkan aplikasi Railfun sebagai platform layanan Multimedia on Demand yang optimal bagi penumpang kereta api, serta mengintegrasikan fitur Chatbot untuk meningkatkan interaksi dan kemudahan pengguna. Aplikasi ini dirancang untuk menyediakan akses offline ke berbagai konten hiburan seperti video, musik, dan permainan, dilengkapi dengan Chatbot sebagai asisten virtual yang intuitif. Hasil evaluasi kepuasan pengguna menunjukkan bahwa 89,68% responden menyatakan puas dengan aplikasi Railfun, yang mengindikasikan kategori 'Sangat Memuaskan'. Diharapkan, Railfun dapat meningkatkan kenyamanan dan kepuasan penumpang selama perjalanan, sekaligus menjadi solusi inovatif dalam meningkatkan kualitas layanan transportasi publik melalui pemanfaatan teknologi digital yang modern dan efisien</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>: Sektor konstruksi informal pada proyek perumahan KPR sering kali menghadapi ketidaksesuaian informasi dan ketidakpastian arus kas yang membebani mandor melalui sistem dana talangan upah pekerja. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk merancang, mengimplementasikan, dan menguji keandalan fungsional aplikasi mobile berbasis No-Code Development Platform (NCDP) AppSheet guna mendigitalisasi manajemen administrasi proyek secara inklusif. Metode penelitian yang diterapkan mengadopsi siklus pengembangan perangkat lunak terstruktur dengan pengujian fungsionalitas sistem menggunakan metode Black-Box Testing. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa arsitektur struktur tabel yang dibangun berhasil mentransformasi pencatatan absensi harian, manajemen kasbon, dan rekapitulasi upah buruh yang semula berbasis kertas menjadi sistem repositori cloud yang terpusat dan dinamis. Evaluasi pengujian membuktikan seluruh fungsi navigasi, validasi input data transaksional, serta otomatisasi formula perhitungan upah bersih berjalan presisi dan bebas dari kesalahan perhitungan, sehingga digitalisasi proses bisnis melalui platform no-code membuktikan bahwa teknologi nir-kode layak menjadi solusi digital terjangkau yang mudah diadopsi oleh para pelaku industri di sektor konstruksi informal.</jats:p>

title: Implementasi Sistem Interaksi Multi Touch untuk Manipulasi Objek 3D Berbasis Augmented Reality
abstract: <jats:p>Augmented Reality (AR) merupakan teknologi yang mampu mengintegrasikan objek virtual ke dalam lingkungan nyata secara real-time sehingga dapat memberikan pengalaman visual yang lebih interaktif. Selain visualisasi objek tiga dimensi, interaksi pengguna terhadap objek virtual menjadi salah satu aspek penting dalam pengembangan aplikasi AR. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengimplementasikan sistem interaksi multi touch untuk manipulasi objek 3D pada aplikasi Augmented Reality berbasis Android. Metode pengembangan yang digunakan adalah Multimedia Development Life Cycle (MDLC) yang terdiri dari tahapan Concept, Design, Material Collecting, Assembly, Testing, dan Distribution, dengan fokus penelitian pada tahap Assembly dan Testing. Implementasi dilakukan menggunakan Unity dan Vuforia, di mana objek 3D ditempatkan pada Image target dan dilengkapi fitur manipulasi berupa rotasi menggunakan satu sentuhan (single touch) serta perubahan skala menggunakan dua sentuhan (pinch gesture). Pengujian dilakukan menggunakan metode Black Box Testing pada perangkat Redmi 13 dengan total 50 skenario pengujian. Hasil pengujian menunjukkan bahwa seluruh skenario berhasil dijalankan sesuai dengan fungsi yang dirancang sehingga memperoleh tingkat keberhasilan sebesar 100%. Berdasarkan hasil tersebut, sistem interaksi multi touch yang diimplementasikan mampu mendukung manipulasi objek 3D secara responsif dan intuitif pada lingkungan Augmented Reality berbasis Android serta berpotensi dikembangkan untuk berbagai kebutuhan aplikasi interaktif di masa mendatang.</jats:p>

title: SEBGen: A Self-Evolving Benchmark Generation Framework for Software Engineering Agents
abstract: <jats:p>Static software engineering benchmarks such as SWE-bench suffer from three fundamental limitations: task sets are fixed and become saturated as model capabilities rapidly improve; expert construction is costly and slow; and difficulty levels cannot adapt to evolving model abilities. We present SEBGen, a self-evolving benchmark generation framework that synthesizes evaluation tasks from code repositories and continuously updates its generation strategies through an evolution loop. SEBGen introduces three key innovations: an explicit five-dimension exploration value evaluator that quantitatively scores generation strategies across quality, novelty, difficulty coverage, skill diversity, and evolution potential, replacing implicit LLM judgments; a hybrid validation pipeline combining three mechanical checks (schema, compile, functional), an LLM-based semantic assessment, and a repeated-judgment gate; and a self-evolving loop with archive-based experience accumulation, sigmoid-scaled parent selection, and LLM-driven strategy mutation. On a synthetic corpus, SEBGen achieves a 96 percent stage-level validation pass rate (E1; 48/50 stage observations) and preserves generation quality through the evolution loop while showing no measurable improvement over a budget-matched non-evolution baseline. On a real repository, it generates candidate benchmark tasks from all six tqdm commits that passed the schema and LLM-based screening stages, although the compile and functional stages could not be executed because these tasks carry no test patch. A judge-level comparison against SWE-bench Lite, partially corroborated by an independent judge from a different model family (Qwen), places generated real repository tasks below expert-constructed tasks (0.48 vs. 0.83 under deepseek-chat; 0.55 vs. 0.78 under qwen-plus, mean of two passes). An extension to two further repositories (requests, flask) achieves 0/4 acceptance across executed screening stages, indicating that the system does not yet transfer reliably beyond the original repository. These results provide proof-of-concept evidence of feasibility: the framework generates candidate tasks automatically, while executable verification of real-repository tasks, reliable self-improvement, and cross-repository transfer remain open problems.</jats:p>

Gated Autonomy: A Layered Security Framework for Tool Access Governance in LLM-Driven Coding Agents
abstract: <jats:p>Large Language Model (LLM)-driven coding agents have evolved from inline code completion utilities into autonomous systems capable of executing shell commands, modifying file hierarchies, retrieving remote documentation, and invoking external APIs. This expanded operational autonomy introduces security vulnerabilities that conventional software permission architectures fail to mediate. In this paper, we examine the attack surface created when autonomous programming agents are granted broad access to system-level tools. We propose Gated Autonomy, an architectural framework that enforces the principle of least privilege across the entire tool-execution lifecycle. The framework couples three defensive layers: a declarative policy gate enforcing static capability boundaries and parameter whitelisting, a runtime context evaluator tracking data provenance and privilege accumulation, and a postexecution audit engine providing counterfactual verification against temporal causal manipulation. We evaluate Gated Autonomy against a comprehensive taxonomy of fifteen documented attack vectors drawn from commercial coding assistants and open-source agent runtimes. Our empirical analysis demonstrates that the framework completely mitigates direct tool hijacking and cross-tool privilege escalation while reducing developer verification interruptions by over 80% through selective escalation.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Perkembangan pesat AI generatif seperti ChatGPT membawa dampak besar pada pendidikan tinggi, terutama dalam sistem pembelajaran terbuka dan jarak jauh (ODL). Penelitian menunjukkan bahwa meskipun ChatGPT menawarkan keuntungan seperti akses informasi cepat, bantuan penulisan, dan personalisasi pembelajaran, penggunaan yang tidak bijak dapat menurunkan motivasi belajar, memicu ketergantungan, serta menghambat berpikir kritis dan kreativitas mahasiswa. Selain itu, muncul tantangan etis seperti plagiarisme, pelanggaran privasi, dan kurangnya literasi AI. Oleh karena itu, diperlukan strategi pemanfaatan AI yang adaptif dan etis untuk mendukung pembelajaran tanpa mengorbankan kemampuan akademik dan intelektual mahasiswa.</jats:p>

Scrub Data: A Framework for Reproducible Data Curation with AI Coding Agents
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                <jats:p>
                  Data curation—the process of collecting, cleaning, and joining raw datasets for unified analysis—is a time-consuming yet crucial part of any data science project. With the emergence of powerful agentic coding tools, it is tempting to “vibe curate—
                  <jats:italic>i</jats:italic>
                  .
                  <jats:italic>e</jats:italic>
                  ., to prompt AI agents to perform data curation operations and blindly trust their outputs in order to finish work more quickly. However, this can exacerbate two key challenges that already plague manual data curation workflows:
                  <jats:bold>reproducibility</jats:bold>
                  —the ability to trace the exact set of modifications applied to raw datasets—and
                  <jats:bold>verifiability</jats:bold>
                  —the ability to audit changes and confirm that data is processed properly. To address these issues, we introduce
                  <jats:bold>Scrub Data</jats:bold>
                  , a framework that enables the use of AI agents in data curation workflows while transparently maintaining both reproducibility and verifiability. The framework involves an interactive data curation loop between a user and an AI agent, backed by a data provenance graph that tracks and versions all dataset updates. The data graph requires that all updates are formatted as self-contained executable steps, allowing any version of a dataset to be reconstructed from raw data by playing forward the transformations stored in the graph. This workflow takes place within a lightweight web application that is designed to be modified by users and agents in real-time to create custom visualization tools for identifying data curation needs and verifying outcomes. We demonstrate the usefulness of the framework with a real data curation use case from animal movement ecology. Starting with 89M raw GPS coordinates, we use the framework to curate a benchmark dataset of 2.5M coordinates to be used for machine learning or statistical analysis. The framework is available for use and extension at
                  <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="https://github.com/justinkay/scrubdata">https://github.com/justinkay/scrubdata</jats:ext-link>
                  .
                </jats:p>

Legacy System Modernization with Coding Agents: A Case Study
abstract: <jats:p>Legacy systems built on discontinued platforms are a recurring technological liability in organizations that depend on these applications to sustain critical business processes. Although modernization is strategically necessary, it is costly and error-prone when performed exclusively through manual effort. In this paper, we report on a case study conducted in a real industrial setting, where we evaluate both the effectiveness and efficiency of AI coding agents in supporting the migration of legacy systems to modern platforms. By using one version of Claude Code agent, we migrated 12 features of distinct complexity levels from a corporate ERP system written in Visual Basic 6 to C# .NET 10 under a single-generation strategy. Once the migration sessions were completed, we measured the equivalence of the migrated features against the original ones, and collected data about the time spent and the number of tokens consumed by the agent during the process. In our experiment, the agent achieved an average equivalence of 70%, with a strong asymmetry across complexity levels; low-level features achieved 92%, and high-complexity ones scored 47%. Similar asymmetry was observed in the cost-based metrics; low-level features consumed 1.47M tokens ($1.66), whereas high-level ones used 9.09M ($10.28). We reveal the practical scenarios and circumstances where this migration strategy is more effective, as well as discuss the limitations and challenges of using AI agents for legacy system modernization.</jats:p>
